Type III is incorrect. It is associated with polyclonal antibodies, usually with rheumatoid factor. Disease associations include rheumatoid arthritis and Sjogren's syndrome.

Type IV
Type IV is not a recognised cryoglobulinaemia classification.

Type V
Type V is also not a recognised classification.

stem: A 44-year-old man attends the genetic clinic after being diagnosed with prostate cancer. He has no other medical history, does not smoke, and is not on any regular medication. His family history is notable for pancreatic cancer in his maternal relatives. What gene mutation is most likely to be present in this man?
explanation:
BRCA2
BRCA2 mutation is associated with prostate cancer in men. BRCA2 is associated with prostate, breast, and pancreatic cancer in men. The man has early-onset prostate cancer with a significant family history of pancreatic cancer making a BRCA2 gene mutation the most likely to be present. Depending on the personal and family history of malignancy, specific screening is advised when a BRCA2 mutation is found, i.e. prostate-specific antigen screening from the age of 40 in all men. The BRCA2 gene is located on the long arm of chromosome 13.

ALK
An ALK gene mutation is associated with adenocarcinoma lung carcinoma. ALK gene mutation-associated lung cancers are associated with younger age and no or little smoking history/exposure. The ALK gene is found on chromosome 2.

C-KIT
A C-KIT is a gene mutation associated with gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GIST) and acute myeloid leukaemia. The c-KIT gene is found in chromosome 4. The most common site of GISTs are the stomach and jejunum/ileum. GI bleeding is the most common presentation of GISTs.

EGFR
Renal cell carcinoma and non-small cell lung carcinoma are associated with EGFR gene mutations. The EGFR gene is found on chromosome 7. EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as osimertinib combined with chemotherapy have been shown to increase progression-free survival.

KRAS
KRAS gene mutations are associated with pancreatic cancers but not prostate cancer. A BRCA2 mutation would be more likely in this case given the personal history of prostate cancer. The KRAS gene is situated on chromosome 12.

stem: A 43-year-old man attended ambulatory care following a general practitioner (GP) referral for anaemia. He has a past history of hypothyroidism for which he takes levothyroxine 75 micrograms once daily. Routine bloods were done at his GP surgery after he attended for a diabetes check as he has a significant family history of this back in India. These were as follows: Hb 110 g/L (135-180) MCV 60 fL (80-96) He denies blood loss, melaena, haematemesis, haematuria or per rectum bleeding. There is no history of weight loss recently and has recently made dietary changes given his concern about diabetes. He drinks around 12 units of alcohol a week. What is the best investigation to determine the underlying pathology?
options: Liver function tests including gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT)
explanation:
Haemoglobin electrophoresis
Disproportionate microcytic anaemia - think beta-thalassaemia trait. Here we have a case of asymptomatic, disproportionate microcytic anaemia in a man of Asian descent. The most likely cause of this is beta thalassaemia trait. Whilst all of the above options are reasonable investigations to request, the haemoglobin electrophoresis is the diagnostic test of choice for beta thalassaemia trait. It would typically show reduced or absent haemoglobin A, increased haemoglobin A2 (>3.5%) and increased haemoglobin F.

Blood film
Blood film would help point to a cause e.g. poikilocytosis or anisocytosis in iron deficiency.

Iron studies
Iron studies would be essential in his workup as it is the most common cause of microcytic anaemia. However, the disproportionate nature of the MCV should point to a potential other cause. In addition, he doesn't have many risk factors for significant iron loss. In beta thalassaemia trait, iron deficiency can co-exist, but typically it would be normal. It is unlikely to be as severe as the MCV would suggest.

Liver function tests including gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT)
Liver function tests including a GGT would be useful in macrocytic anaemia to see if alcohol would be the main contributor to a patient's anaemia.

Thyroid function tests
Thyroid function tests would be useful to exclude this as a contributor. Hypothyroidism could cause a normocytic or macrocytic anaemia typically.

stem: A 60-year-old male is brought in by his concerned son. The patient is known to have advanced, non-small cell lung cancer and is currently under review for palliative radiotherapy. Over the last 2 days, he has experienced increasing weakness of his legs confining him to his bed. On direct questioning, he reports ongoing chest discomfort, breathlessness and sweating at night for several months. He has also noticed some difficulty passing urine associated with the weakness. On exam, he has global reduced power of the legs with increased ankle and knee reflexes. His observations are seen below: HR 80 /min, BP 142/80 mmHg, RR 25 /min, Oxygen sats 95%, Temperature 37.6 ºC. What is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?
explanation:
High-dose oral dexamethasone
If neoplastic spinal cord compression is suspected, high-dose oral dexamethasone should be given whilst awaiting investigations. This patient has presented with possible cord compression and therefore urgent high-dose dexamethasone must be given to reduce possible oedema and prevent further swelling and spinal injury. The patient's features of lower motor neurone signs and increased reflexes, along with an established diagnosis of lung cancer means he is at risk of possible spinal metastases and should be managed as such until proven otherwise. Spinal cord compression is an oncological emergency and so dexamethasone should be given whilst arranging investigations, ideally a whole MRI spine within 24 hours of presentation.

Broad spectrum antibiotics
Although the patient is at increased suspectable given his cancer there is no clear indication of infection. Night sweating is a common feature of various cancers and is not necessarily a sign of infection and the patient's urinary issues are likely due to neurogenic bladder secondary to spinal cord compression. The patient denies any specific infective symptoms and is haemodynamically stable making the likelihood of sepsis low, particularly when compared to the risk of spinal cord compression. IV antibiotics can be considered especially if further evidence of infection is found (e.g. raised inflammatory markers, positive urine dip) but for now high dose steroids in the form of dexamethasone is the priority.

IV mannitol
IV mannitol is often used in patients presenting with another oncological emergency, raised intracranial pressure, which can occur due to brain metastases. Although brain metastases present with neurological signs it would be very unusual for this to occur without local cerebral symptoms such as headache, vomiting, altered mental state etc. Also, high dose dexamethasone would be the recommended first treatment before considering mannitol in these cases anyway.

Urgent MRI whole spine
A whole MRI spine is an important aspect of management and should ideally be carried out within 24 hours in suspected spinal cord compression however dexamethasone should be given whilst this investigation is being arranged. Spinal cord compression is time-critical and the commencement of dexamethasone should be a priority.

Urgent referral for radiotherapy
A referral for radiotherapy may be appropriate at a later stage however this is not the initial management. Confirmation of spinal metastases and an oncological opinion must be sought prior to radiotherapy, all of which can take time. Dexamethasone can be given immediately within the emergency department and can improve outcomes by reducing further spinal cord compression.

stem: You are reviewing a 75-year-old patient, presenting with shortness of breath, lethargy, night sweats, weight loss, and aches in her bones over the past 2 months. She also reports that she has been suffering from frequent epistaxis and recurrent skin infections. She had a stroke with unknown cause one year ago and reports experiencing intense pruritis especially after a hot shower and her skin appearing red and flushed over the past year. Examination is unremarkable other than splenomegaly. Given the probable underlying condition, what is the most likely cause of her new symptoms?
explanation:
Acute myeloid leukaemia
Acute myeloid leukaemia is correct. The underlying diagnosis referred to is polycythaemia rubra vera, a myeloproliferative disorder caused by clonal proliferation of a marrow stem cell leading to an increase in red cell volume, often accompanied by overproduction of neutrophils and platelets. This can present with pruritis, flushing, splenomegaly, haemorrhage due to defective platelet function, splenomegaly and hyperviscosity - hence the patient presenting previously with a stroke of unknown cause, pruritus and flushing. This is most common in patients in their sixties. In 5-15% of cases, this can progress to myelofibrosis or acute myeloid leukaemia (AML). Here the patient is presenting with symptoms of AML including anaemia - lethargy and shortness of breath, neutropenia - recurrent infections, thrombocytopenia with the epistaxis, night sweats, weight loss and bone pain.

Aplastic anaemia
Aplastic anaemia is incorrect, this does fit with the anaemia symptoms but does not explain the thrombocytopenia, or the long-standing symptoms.

Chronic myeloid leukaemia
Chronic myeloid leukaemia can present similarly to AML, but it does not fit well with the underlying long-standing diagnosis of polycythemia rubra vera.

Feltys syndrome
Felty's syndrome is a triad of low neutrophils, splenomegaly and rheumatoid arthritis. This could explain the splenomegaly and achy bones but it does not account for the other symptoms.

HIV
HIV can also present with night sweats, weight loss, and recurrent infections due to the immune system being compromised. However, this does not fit well the longer standing symptoms of pruritis, flushing, and previous stroke.

stem: A 46-year-old woman is being reviewed in the breast cancer multidisciplinary team meeting. After reviewing her history, imaging and histology, the team decide that the best chemotherapy agent to commence her on is docetaxel. She is counselled appropriately regarding the side effects and agrees to start. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
explanation:
Prevents microtubule depolymerisation
Taxanes such as docetaxel - prevents microtubule depolymerisation & disassembly, decreasing free tubulin. By doing so, and preventing disassembly, docetaxel leads to a decrease in free tubulin.

Blocks thymidylate synthase
Blocking thymidylate synthase refers to the action of fluorouracil, a pyrimidine analogue that induces cell cycle arrest and apoptosis. Adverse effects include myelosuppression, mucositis and dermatitis.

Cross-links DNA
Cross-linking DNA is the method of action of cyclophosphamide, an alkylating agent. It is known for causing haemorrhagic cystitis, which can be prevented with adjunctive use of the drug mesna.

Inhibits ribonucleotide reductase
Inhibition of ribonucleotide reductase refers to the action of hydroxyurea, thereby decreasing DNA synthesis. Side effects include myelosuppression.

Stabilises DNA-topoisomerase II complex
Stabilisation of the DNA-topoisomerase II complex refers to the action of doxorubicin and the anthracycline class. These are known to lead to cardiomyopathy.

stem: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with facial swelling. He lives in social care, and one of his carers called an ambulance after noticing his face had started to swell over the last 24 hours. On arrival, the crew administered adrenaline with minimal effect. On examination, he has diffuse swelling of his face, in particular his lips and tongue. There is no rash seen. He does not report any itching. The following day the swelling had improved. He was discharged with follow-up in the immunology clinic 2 weeks later. At the clinic, what investigation is most appropriate to identify the diagnosis?
explanation:
C4
C4 is the best screening test for hereditary angioedema in between attacks. A result of low C4 would support the diagnosis.

C1
C1 is incorrect. Instead, it is measuring the C1 inhibitor (C1-INH) level which is appropriate for the diagnosis of hereditary angioedema.

C2
C2 is incorrect. Although levels are also frequently low between attacks, C2 is less reliable compared to C4.

C3
C3 is incorrect. C3 is often low in autoimmune disease but should be normal in hereditary angioedema.

Mast cell tryptase
Mast cell tryptase is incorrect. This is the investigation of choice when an anaphylactic reaction is likely. Guidance is that levels should be taken at the time of the reaction, as soon as possible after emergency treatment has commenced, with a second level taken ideally within one to two hours (but no later than four). The absence of itch, rash and response to adrenaline all make anaphylaxis less likely in this case.

stem: Which of the following is a good prognostic factor in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia?
explanation:
Female sex
The correct answer is Female sex. Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) prognosis is generally better in females than in males. Several studies have shown that women with CLL tend to live longer and have a slower disease progression compared to men, although the exact reasons for this gender difference are not fully understood.

Lymphocyte doubling time < 12 months
Lymphocyte doubling time < 12 months is not a good prognostic factor. In fact, it's quite the opposite. A shorter lymphocyte doubling time (less than 12 months) suggests a more aggressive disease and poorer prognosis. Patients with CLL who have a lymphocyte doubling time of less than 12 months are typically at a higher risk of disease progression and may require treatment sooner.

CD38 expression positive
CD38 expression positive is also associated with a worse prognosis in CLL. CD38 is a cell surface protein that is often overexpressed in certain types of cancer, including CLL. Studies have found that patients with CLL who test positive for CD38 expression tend to have a more aggressive disease course and poorer overall survival compared to those who are CD38-negative.

Age > 70 years
Age > 70 years is not considered a good prognostic factor either. Older age at diagnosis (>70 years) has been associated with worse outcomes in CLL, likely due to comorbidities and decreased tolerance to treatment.

Raised LDH
Raised LDH (lactate dehydrogenase) levels can indicate high tumour burden or rapid cell turnover, both of which suggest more aggressive disease and thus poorer prognosis. Elevated LDH levels are commonly seen in many types of cancer, including CLL, and are often associated with advanced disease stage and worse survival outcomes.

stem: You are asked to review a 60-year-old Greek man with known glucose-6phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency who was admitted with malaria and a chest infection. He has developed jaundice and haemolytic anaemia after starting some medications this morning. Which of these medications are most likely to have precipitated his crisis?
explanation:
Primaquine
Primaquine is a well known cause of haemolysis in G6PD deficiency and is used in the treatment of malaria.

Clarithromycin
Penicillins and macrolides are safe antibiotics to use in G6PD deficiency.

Amoxicillin
Penicillins and macrolides are safe antibiotics to use in G6PD deficiency.

Artesunate
Artesunate is generally considered safe to use in G6PD deficiency.

stem: A 54-year-old man is investigated for recurrent episodes of abdominal pain associated with weakness of his arms and legs. Which one of the following urine tests would best indicate lead toxicity?
explanation:
Coproporphyrin
The correct answer is Coproporphyrin. Lead toxicity, also known as plumbism, interferes with heme synthesis and results in increased urinary excretion of coproporphyrin III. This is a common diagnostic test for lead poisoning. The patient's symptoms of abdominal pain and weakness could be indicative of lead colic and peripheral neuropathy respectively, both of which are associated with lead toxicity.

Haemoglobinuria
Haemoglobinuria refers to the presence of haemoglobin in the urine. It is not directly related to lead toxicity but can occur due to various conditions such as severe burns, infections, transfusion reactions or certain medications. Haemoglobinuria can cause the urine to have a dark, reddish or cola colour.

Porphobilinogen
Porphobilinogen is usually increased in acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) and hereditary coproporphyria (HCP), not in lead toxicity. AIP and HCP are types of porphyria that present with neurological symptoms and abdominal pain but they are not caused by an external toxin like lead.

Uroporphyrin
Uroporphyrin levels may be elevated in porphyrias such as porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) or congenital erythropoietic porphyria (CEP). These conditions can cause skin sensitivity to sunlight and other symptoms but they are not related to lead exposure.

Ham's test
Ham's test, also known as the acidified serum lysis test, is used to diagnose paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH). PNH is a rare acquired disorder that leads to the destruction of red blood cells, causing haemoglobinuria, especially at night or early morning. It does not indicate exposure to any specific toxins like lead.

stem: A 67-year-old man is diagnosed with myelofibrosis. What is the most common presenting symptom of myelofibrosis?
explanation:
Lethargy
Myelofibrosis is a myeloproliferative neoplasm characterised by bone marrow fibrosis and extramedullary haematopoiesis. It often presents with non-specific symptoms due to anaemia, the most common of which is lethargy. As the disease progresses, patients may experience increasing fatigue and weakness, largely due to ineffective erythropoiesis leading to anaemia.

Anorexia and weight loss
Anorexia and weight loss can be seen in myelofibrosis but are not typically the most common presenting symptom. These symptoms are usually indicative of advanced disease or transformation into acute leukaemia, which occurs in a minority of patients.

Night sweats
Night sweats are another possible symptom of myelofibrosis, often associated with systemic symptoms like fever and weight loss. However, they are also more commonly seen in other conditions such as lymphomas or infections like tuberculosis.

Easy bruising
Easy bruising (Ecchymosis) can occur in myelofibrosis due to platelet dysfunction or thrombocytopenia. However, this is generally less common than symptoms related to anaemia such as lethargy. Additionally, easy bruising tends to be more characteristic of diseases primarily involving platelets rather than being a primary feature of myelofibrosis.

Splenomegaly
Splenomegaly, while it is a common physical finding in myelofibrosis due to extramedullary haematopoiesis, it might not be symptomatic initially. Patients often present with left upper quadrant discomfort only when the spleen becomes significantly enlarged over time.

stem: A 25-year-old woman reports that she gets tingling, itching and swelling of her lips within minutes of eating uncooked apple. There is no rash, breathing difficulty or gastrointestinal upset. The symptoms tend to last 1-2 hours before improving after taking an oral antihistamine. She adds that she is able to eat apple pie without any symptoms. She has a history of irritable bowel syndrome and hayfever. She is not on any regular medication but takes cetirizine during the summer months. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Oral allergy syndrome
Itching and tingling of the lips, tongue and mouth are the most common symptoms of oral allergy syndrome. These symptoms are in keeping with oral allergy syndrome (also known as pollen food syndrome). This is due to cross-reactivity of allergens found in both pollen (hence it is seen in people with hayfever) and certain raw fruits and vegetables. The history of symptoms after ingestion of the raw food, but little or no symptoms after eating the cooked version, is typical. This is due to the denaturation of the allergen protein during the heating process.

Anaphylactoid reaction
Anaphylactoid reactions describe those which produce the same clinical picture as anaphylaxis but are non-IgE mediated. This characteristically occurs with agents such as contrast media, aspirin and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, which can cause a direct breakdown of the mast cells and basophils without needing previous sensitisation. Meanwhile, oral allergy syndrome is an IgE-mediated condition.

Contact dermatitis
Contact dermatitis is a form of eczema caused by direct contact of a specific allergen with the skin. Common substances include nickel and adhesive plasters, rather than foods. It is mediated by a type 4 (delayed) hypersensitivity reaction and usually occurs 48-72 hours after exposure to the allergen.

Hereditary angioedema
Hereditary angioedema is an autosomal dominant disorder that results in recurrent attacks of severe swelling which can occur spontaneously or following minor trauma or stress. It is not triggered by food.

Mast cell activation syndrome
Mast cell activation syndrome is a condition causing recurrent episodes of allergy symptoms such as urticaria, swelling, breathing difficulties, tachycardia and diarrhoea, mediated by the release of mast cell mediators during attacks. It is still a poorly understood condition, but is often idiopathic and not linked to exposure to a particular allergen.

stem: Transmission of which type of infection is most likely to occur following a platelet transfusion?
explanation:
Bacterial
Platelet transfusions are at particular risk of bacterial contamination as they are stored at room temperature. As platelet concentrates are generally stored at room temperature they provide a more favourable environment for bacterial contamination than other blood products.

stem: A 36-year-old woman attends the emergency department with a 2 hour history of left sided arm and leg weakness. She reports a 5 day history of fatigue, dizziness and nausea. She has never had anything like this before. She has no relevant medical history, or family history of autoimmune disease. On examination, she had multiple petechiae on her legs bilaterally. She is able to talk in full sentences and shows no signs of higher cognitive deficit. She has 4/5 power on her left arm and leg, with no sensory deficit. She has no cranial nerve abnormalities. Her observations were as follows: Blood pressure - 161/93mmHg, heart rate - 75bpm, temperature 38.2ºC, oxygen saturations - 97% on air, respiratory rate - 18/min. Hb 82 g/L Female: (115 160) Platelets 21 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 8.7 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Prothrombin time (PT) 12 secs (10-14 secs) Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) 25 secs (25-35 secs) Reticulocytes 6% (0.5 - 1.5) Urea 20.1 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 201 µmol/L (55 - 120) Blood film showed schistocytosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
TTP presents with a pentad of fever, neuro signs, thrombocytopenia, haemolytic anaemia and renal failure. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) is a thrombotic microangiopathy that arises from reduced von Willebrand factor-cleaving proteases (ADAMTS13). This process is autoimmune in 95% of cases and is labelled as acquired. Thrombi that form from platelets in the small vessels cause resultant thrombocytopenia with a risk of occlusion of end-organ vasculature, which may result in neurological, gastrointestinal, renal and cardiac symptoms. The classic pentad only occurs in 5% of cases. Mechanical sheering results in haemolytic anaemia. TTP is typically diagnosed with a combination of clinical findings and ADAMTS13 testing. Schistocytosis on the blood film suggests erythrocyte fragment shearing and is secondary to TTP/DIC/HUS.

Haemolytic uraemic syndrome
Haemolytic-uraemic syndrome (HUS) is an important differential as it is also a thrombotic microangiopathy, and so can present with multi-organ dysfunction, thrombocytopenia and haemolytic anaemia. However, it is typically preceded by a period of diarrhoea and abdominal pain. If the diagnosis is unclear, ADAMTS13 assays should be done.

Antiphospholipid syndrome
Antiphospholipid syndrome is an autoimmune procoagulant state characterised by venous and/or arterial thromboses. While it can cause stroke due to vascular occlusion, it does not cause purpura or schistocytosis.

Disseminated intravascular coagulation
Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is an important differential as it can cause similar symptoms, including renal failure, purpura, thrombocytopenia and neurological/GI/cardiac compromise. However, given the normal bleeding profile, it is less likely to be the case.

Malignant hypertension
Malignant hypertension can cause a microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, as well as renal failure with thrombocytopenia, however, it is typically characterised by a blood pressure of >180/120mmHg, and would not cause purpura.

stem: A 25-year-old man is admitted to the haematology ward. He was recently diagnosed with Burkitt's lymphoma and received his first dose of chemotherapy today. Blood results from today are as follows: Na+ 138 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 6.2 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Bicarbonate 22 mmol/L (22 - 29) Urea 10.8 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 162 µmol/L (55 - 120) Calcium 1.9 mmol/L (2.1-2.6) Phosphate 2.8 mmol/L (0.8-1.4) Blood results from yesterday are as follows: Na+ 135 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 3.5 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Bicarbonate 24 mmol/L (22 - 29) Urea 4.8 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 72 µmol/L (55 - 120) Calcium 2.4 mmol/L (2.1-2.6) Phosphate 2.4 mmol/L (0.8-1.4) What treatment is required?
explanation:
Treatment dose rasburicase
Treatment dose rasburicase is correct. The patient has clinical TLS and thus needs emergency treatment with rasburicase. This should be at the higher treatment dose of 200 micrograms/kg. This drug is a recombinant form of mammalian urate oxidase. It metabolises urate to allantoin, a substance 10x more soluble than uric acid. It acts immediately on any uric acid that is already formed. For this reason, it is the most effective drug used in the management of TLS.

Allopurinol
Allopurinol is incorrect. This drug reduces the production of uric acid by decreasing the rate of conversion of hypoxanthine to xanthine, and of xanthine to uric acid. Both hypoxanthine and xanthine are more soluble than uric acid and so less precipitation occurs in the renal tubules. However, it does not increase the rate of breakdown of uric acid that is already present so its therapeutic effect is delayed by 24-72 hours. Thus rasburicase is the preferred agent for the management of TLS due to its immediate therapeutic effect.

Calcium gluconate
Calcium gluconate is incorrect. Indications for calcium gluconate include severe hyperkalaemia, or symptomatic hypocalcaemia, neither of which are present in this clinical case.

Phosphate binder
Phosphate binder is incorrect. Although a phosphate binder could be used in this scenario, the priority is to reduce the levels of uric acid with rasburicase.

Prophylactic dose rasburicase
Prophylactic dose rasburicase is incorrect. A low dose of rasburicase (e.g. 3mg) is often used in high-risk patients to prevent TLS. However, the patient, in this case, has established clinical TLS and thus requires a higher treatment dose.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with a history of recurrent chest and sinus infections since childhood. She has a past medical history of two episodes of pneumonia that have required admission for intravenous antibiotics. Currently, she appears well on examination and there are no specific findings. She is referred for blood tests: Hb 112 g/L (115 - 160) Platelets 343 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 5.6 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Serum IgG Low Serum IgA Low Serum IgM Low What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID)
Common variable immunodeficiency - low antibody levels, specifically in immunoglobulin types IgG, IgM and IgA. → recurrent chest and other infections This patient's presentation fits most with CVID. This is an immune disorder characterised by recurrent infections and low levels of immunoglobulins IgA, IgG, and IgM. It is caused by a variety of possible genetic mutations. The condition is typically not diagnosed until adulthood when patients present with a longstanding history of frequent infections. Treatment usually involves lifelong immunoglobulin replacement therapy.

Bruton's agammaglobulinaemia
Bruton's agammaglobulinaemia is a rare X-linked recessive immune disorder resulting in poor B-cell development. Whilst it also presents with recurrent infections and low immunoglobulins of all classes, it is much less common overall than CVID and mainly affects male patients due to the X-linked nature of its inheritance.

DiGeorge syndrome
DiGeorge syndrome is a genetic condition affecting T-cell development. Patients also commonly have congenital heart disease, learning difficulties, and cleft palate, none of which are present here.

Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID)
SCID, as the name implies, is a much more severe immunodeficiency than the presentation described here, affecting both T-cells and B-cells. The most common form is X-linked SCID, usually due to mutations in the gene coding the common gamma chain of multiple interleukin receptors. Patients are afflicted with significant infections from infancy and do not survive into childhood unless the condition is diagnosed early and treated with bone marrow transplantation.

Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, like SCID, also affects both T-cells and B-cells. As well as recurrent infections, it is also linked to eczema and thrombocytopaenia, which are not described here. However, it is X-linked recessive, making it much less likely than CVID in this scenario.

stem: A 72-year-old woman is admitted with confusion and pallor. Her daughter reports that she has been getting more confused and tired for the past three months. Blood tests are reported as follows: Hb 89 g/l MCV 125 fl Plt 148 * 109/l WBC 4.4 * 109/l In light of the macrocytic anaemia some further tests are ordered: Intrinsic factor antibodies Negative Vitamin B12 94 ng/l (200-900 ng/l) Folic acid 1.1 nmol/l (> 3.0 nmol/l) What is the most appropriate management?
options: Oral folic acid + start Intramuscular vitamin B12 when folic acid levels are normal
Intramuscular vitamin B12 + start oral folic acid when vitamin B12 levels are normal
explanation:
Intramuscular vitamin B12 + start oral folic acid when vitamin B12 levels are normal
The correct answer is Intramuscular vitamin B12 + start oral folic acid when vitamin B12 levels are normal. This patient presents with a megaloblastic anaemia (evidenced by high MCV of 125 fl) with both vitamin B12 and folate deficiency. In cases of combined deficiency, it is crucial to replace vitamin B12 first. This is because giving folate alone in vitamin B12 deficiency can precipitate or worsen neurological complications (subacute combined degeneration of the cord) while masking the haematological features of B12 deficiency. The initial treatment should be intramuscular hydroxocobalamin, typically given as 1mg on alternate days for 2 weeks in haematological abnormality without neurological involvement. Once B12 levels have normalised, folate replacement can begin.

Oral folic acid + blood transfusion
Oral folic acid + blood transfusion would be inappropriate as starting folic acid before correcting B12 deficiency could be dangerous for the reasons stated above. While the patient is anaemic, transfusion is not typically necessary unless there are symptoms of severe anaemia or cardiovascular compromise.

Oral folic acid + start Intramuscular vitamin B12 when folic acid levels are normal
Oral folic acid + start Intramuscular vitamin B12 when folic acid levels are normal is incorrect for the same reason - B12 must be replaced first to prevent neurological complications.

Blood transfusion
Blood transfusion alone would not address the underlying vitamin deficiencies. Transfusion should be reserved for patients with severe symptomatic anaemia or cardiovascular compromise.

Oral prednisolone
Oral prednisolone would not be appropriate as this is not an autoimmune condition. While pernicious anaemia (which causes B12 deficiency) has an autoimmune basis, the treatment is still B12 replacement, not immunosuppression. This patient's negative intrinsic factor antibodies also make pernicious anaemia less likely.

stem: A 65-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a one-week history of fatigue and shortness of breath. The examination was unremarkable. In particular, there is no evidence of bleeding on systematic inquiry or examination. Blood results are as follows: Hb 82 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Reticulocytes 442 * 109/L (50-100) Platelets 162 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 12.8 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Bilirubin 66 µmol/L (3 - 17) ALP 42 u/L (30 - 100) ALT 28 u/L (3 - 40) Î³GT 44 u/L (8 - 60) Albumin 36 g/L (35 - 50) What abnormality would be in keeping with the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Low haptoglobin
Haptoglobin binds to free haemoglobin. Anaemia with reticulocytosis is suggestive of haemolysis or bleeding. The markedly raised bilirubin with otherwise normal LFTs is more in keeping with haemolysis, however, it is important to remember that haemorrhage can also result in increased bilirubin levels. Haemolysis results in the release of free haemoglobin. Haptoglobin is produced in the liver, and its primary function is to bind to free haemoglobin. Therefore low haptoglobins is a key feature of haemolysis.

Low ADAMTS13 level
A low ADAMTS13 level would confirm the diagnosis of TTP, which is not the likely diagnosis in this case.

Low LDH
Haemolysis is associated with a raised LDH (due to increased cell turnover), rather than a low LDH.

Negative DAT
A positive DAT (rather than a negative DAT) is associated with autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. However, it is important to remember that there are a wide variety of causes of haemolysis including both immune and non-immune mediated mechanisms.

Raised haptoglobin
Raised haptoglobin is not a feature of haemolysis. Low haptoglobin is the key feature.

stem: A 61-year-old presents for review. She has been having atypical lower back pain for the past two months. An x-ray of her lumbar spine reported raised the possibility of spinal metastases but there is no current evidence of a primary tumour. A series of tumour markers were sent. Which one of the following is most associated with raised levels of CA 15-3?
explanation:
Breast cancer
CA 15-3 is a tumour marker in breast cancers. CA 15-3 (cancer antigen 15-3) is a protein that is produced by normal breast cells and can be found at higher levels in the blood of individuals with breast cancer. It is primarily used as a marker to monitor the response to treatment in patients with advanced breast cancer, although it may also be elevated in other malignancies and benign conditions. It should be noted that CA 15-3 is not recommended for screening or early diagnosis of breast cancer due to its low sensitivity and specificity.

Pancreatic cancer
Pancreatic cancer typically presents with elevated levels of CA 19-9, which is a carbohydrate antigen that can also be raised in gastrointestinal malignancies such as cholangiocarcinoma and colorectal cancer. However, CA 19-9 has limited utility as a diagnostic tool due to its low sensitivity and specificity.

Colorectal cancer
Colorectal cancer can present with elevated levels of carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), which may also be raised in other malignancies such as pancreatic, gastric, and lung cancers. CEA is most commonly used for monitoring disease progression or recurrence after treatment rather than for initial diagnosis.

Ovarian cancer
Ovarian cancer is associated with raised levels of CA 125, a glycoprotein that can also be elevated in endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease, and during menstruation. As with other tumour markers mentioned earlier, CA 125 has limited utility as a diagnostic tool due to its low sensitivity and specificity.

Hepatocellular carcinoma
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) often presents with increased serum levels of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). AFP can also be elevated in germ cell tumours and during pregnancy. While AFP has some utility as a diagnostic tool for HCC, it is primarily used for monitoring response to treatment and detecting recurrence.

stem: A 36-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with fatigue. She has a past medical history of well-controlled rheumatoid arthritis and takes hydroxychloroquine. She does not smoke cigarettes. She drinks approximately one bottle of wine per week. The examination is unremarkable and there is no clinical evidence of synovitis. Blood results demonstrate: Hb 106 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) MCV 62 fl (80-100) MCH 20 pg/cell (27-32) Platelets 189 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 6.2 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Neuts 3.5* 109/L (2.0 - 7.0) Ferritin 540 ng/ml (12-30) Total iron binding capacity 30 µmol/L (45-82) Vitamin B 12 550 ng/ml (200-900) Serum folate 8 ng/ml (2.5-20) Na+ 137 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 4.2 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Bicarbonate 24 mmol/L (22 - 29) Urea 5.2 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 67 µmol/L (55 - 120) TSH 0.4 miU/L (0.2 - 5.5) CRP 4 mg/L (<5) What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Beta-thalassaemia trait
Beta-thalassaemia trait is correct. The haematological findings of this condition typically reflect a mild iron deficiency with a microcytosis out of keeping to the degree of anaemia. It is associated with an increase in iron and therefore serum ferritin may be increased and total iron-binding capacity may be decreased.

Anaemia of chronic disease
Anaemia of chronic disease is incorrect. While she does have rheumatoid arthritis and this is a cause of anaemia of chronic disease, the profound microcytosis out of proportion to the degree of anaemia is more in keeping with thalassaemia trait. Furthermore, we are told her disease is well controlled, making chronic active inflammation less likely.

Haemochromatosis
Haemochromatosis is incorrect. The serum ferritin is elevated but this condition is not typically associated with microcytic anaemia. Furthermore, it usually presents post menopause in female patients.

Iron deficiency anaemia
Iron deficiency anaemia is incorrect. The serum ferritin is raised with a normal CRP. This makes iron deficiency unlikely.

Sideroblastic anaemia
Sideroblastic anaemia is incorrect. This is a rare cause of microcytic anaemia. Alcohol use can be an acquired cause. However, the microcytosis is not typically as profound as the one observed in this case and she drinks within the recommended guidelines, making this diagnosis unlikely. It is also associated with the development of hepatosplenomegaly, which is not mentioned here.

stem: Which one of the following therapeutic options is least recognised in the treatment of aplastic anaemia?
explanation:
Interferon-alpha
The correct answer is Interferon-alpha. Interferon-alpha is not a recognised treatment for aplastic anaemia. Aplastic anaemia is a condition that occurs when the body stops producing enough new blood cells. It's often treated with medications, blood transfusions or stem cell transplants. However, interferon-alpha isn't typically used in the management of this condition.

Stem cell transplantation
Stem cell transplantation is indeed a recognised treatment for aplastic anaemia, particularly for younger patients and those with severe or very severe aplastic anaemia. The procedure involves replacing the patient's bone marrow (which isn't producing sufficient blood cells) with healthy stem cells from a donor.

Anti-lymphocyte globulin
Anti-lymphocyte globulin is another recognised therapeutic option for aplastic anaemia. These are immunosuppressive therapies that work by reducing the body's immune response, which can help increase the production of new blood cells in patients with this condition.

Anti-thymocyte globulin
Anti-thymocyte globulin is another recognised therapeutic option for aplastic anaemia. These are immunosuppressive therapies that work by reducing the body's immune response, which can help increase the production of new blood cells in patients with this condition.

Platelet transfusion
Platelet transfusion is also a common therapeutic option in managing aplastic anaemia. Patients with this condition often have low platelet counts which can lead to bleeding problems. Transfusing platelets can help manage these symptoms and prevent serious bleeding events.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with three months of urinary hesitancy. He has no past medical history. Both of his sisters developed breast cancer before the age of 30. He is of Ashkenazi Jewish heritage. On digital rectal examination, there is an irregular, craggy prostate. What gene likely has a mutation?
explanation:
BRCA2
BRCA2 mutation is associated with prostate cancer in men. The patient presents with obstructive urinary symptoms and a frankly abnormal prostate exam. This suggests prostate cancer is the cause. The history of multiple siblings with early-onset breast cancer suggests a family history of the BRCA mutation. It is BRCA2 rather than BRCA1 that confers an increased risk of prostate cancer in men. This mutation is more common in those with Ashkenazi Jewish heritage.

APC
APC is incorrect. A mutation in this gene is associated with Gardener syndrome which causes multiple colonic polyps along with skull osteomas, thyroid cancer, and epidermoid cysts. Prostate cancer is not a feature and so this is not correct.

BRCA1
BRCA1 is incorrect. This is associated with early-onset breast cancer but it is BRCA2 rather than BRCA1 that causes an increased risk of prostate cancer.

MLH1
MLH1 is incorrect. This encodes a DNA mismatch repair protein. A mutation in this gene causes 'Lynch syndrome', which is a hereditary colorectal cancer syndrome. It is not a cause of prostate cancer.

P53
p53 is incorrect. A mutation in this gene is associated with Li-Fraumeni syndrome. This causes a high incidence of sarcomas and leukaemia rather than prostate cancer.

stem: A 59-year-old woman has presented to the emergency department following a fall. Plain radiographs have confirmed a left hip fracture. She has a history of breast cancer, type 2 diabetes, hypercholesterolaemia and recurrent urinary tract infections. Which of the following drugs that she is taking is most likely to have contributed towards her hip fracture?
explanation:
Letrozole
Letrozole is an aromatase inhibitor that reduces peripheral oestrogen synthesis by blocking the conversion of androgens into oestrogen. It is used in the treatment of oestrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women. This helps to prevent oestrogen-mediated growth stimulation in cancer tissues. In postmenopausal women, oestrogens are mainly derived from the action of the aromatase enzyme; ovarian synthesis of oestrogen has ceased. The inhibition of oestrogen production subsequently increases the risk of osteoporosis which can predispose to fractures. Hence it is advised to assess bone mineral density before letrozole treatment and at regular intervals.

Fenofibrate
Fenofibrate has not been associated with increased fracture risk.

Methenamine hippurate
Methenamine hippurate has not been associated with increased fracture risk.

Nitrofurantoin
Nitrofurantoin has not been associated with increased fracture risk.

Sitagliptin
Sitagliptin has not been associated with increased fracture risk.

stem: A 51-year-old female is referred to the haematology clinic with a haemoglobin of 19.2 g/dl. She is a non-smoker. Her oxygen saturations on room air are 98% and she is noted to have mass in the left upper quadrant. What is the most useful test to establish whether she has polycythaemia vera?
explanation:
JAK2 mutation screen
According to British Society for Haematology guidelines, testing for JAK2 V617F mutation is the initial investigation of choice in suspected polycythaemia vera (PV). JAK2 mutation screen is positive in approximately 95% of PV cases, making it highly sensitive and specific. The presence of JAK2 V617F or exon 12 mutations is now a major diagnostic criterion for PV in the WHO classification. The clinical scenario strongly suggests PV given the elevated haemoglobin, normal oxygen saturations (ruling out hypoxic drive), and presence of splenomegaly (the left upper quadrant mass). In this context, JAK2 mutation testing is the most appropriate initial investigation to confirm the diagnosis.

Bone marrow aspiration
Bone marrow aspiration is not the most useful initial test as it is invasive and should only be performed after JAK2 mutation testing. While bone marrow examination can show characteristic features of PV such as panmyelosis and reduced iron stores, it is typically reserved for cases where the diagnosis remains unclear after initial investigations or when transformation is suspected.

Blood film
Blood film, while useful in the overall assessment, is not specific enough to establish the diagnosis of PV. It may show features such as increased red cells and sometimes basophilia, but these findings are non-specific and can be seen in other conditions including secondary polycythaemia.

Red cell mass
Red cell mass measurement was historically important in diagnosing PV but is now rarely performed. It has been largely superseded by haemoglobin concentration and haematocrit measurements, combined with JAK2 mutation testing, as these are more readily available and provide sufficient diagnostic information.

Transferrin saturation
Transferrin saturation is not particularly useful in establishing the diagnosis of PV. While iron studies may be altered in PV (typically showing low iron and ferritin due to increased red cell production), these changes are non-specific and can occur in many other conditions. The finding would not definitively establish the diagnosis of PV.

stem: Of the following options, which one is the best diagnostic test for paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria?
options: Flow cytometry for CD59 and CD55
explanation:
Flow cytometry for CD59 and CD55
Flow cytometry for CD59 and CD55 is the gold standard test for paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria. Flow cytometry of blood to detect low levels of CD59 and CD55 has now replaced Ham's test as the gold standard investigation in paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.

stem: A 30-year-old female presents with a painless rash on both lower limbs and prolonged gum bleeding this morning whilst brushing her teeth. She has no medical history nor any regular medication. She is apyrexial and her vital signs are within the normal ranges. Clinical examination revealed multiple lower limb petechiae measuring 1-4mm in size. There were no lesions nor active bleeding in the oral cavity. Clinical examination was otherwise normal. Blood tests show: Hb 126 g/L (115 - 160) Platelets 26 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 7.2 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Clotting screen Normal U&Es Normal HCV, HBV, HIV Negative Peripheral blood smear True thrombocytopenia Pregnancy test Negative Which is the most appropriate initial treatment for her condition?
explanation:
Oral prednisolone
First-line treatment for ITP is oral prednisolone. This is a typical presentation of an uncomplicated case of primary immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). Reversible causes of ITP have been excluded by the investigations. From the options provided the appropriate first-line treatment for this case will be oral prednisolone. Corticosteroids help suppress the immune-mediated destruction of platelets.

Intravenous corticosteroids
Intravenous immunoglobulins is a second-line therapy for minor bleeding, or first-line (along with other agents) for severe bleeding. This patient only has features suggesting minor bleeding.

Intravenous immunoglobulins
Intravenous immunoglobulins is a second-line therapy for minor bleeding, or first-line (along with other agents) for severe bleeding. This patient only has features suggesting minor bleeding.

Observation only
Observation only is reserved for asymptomatic adults with a platelet count >=30 * 109/L. This patient has a platelet count <30 * 109/L and also has petechiae with mild mucosal bleeding, therefore not asymptomatic, and requires treatment due to increased bleeding risk with the low platelet count.

Platelet transfusion
Platelet transfusions are reserved for those with life- or organ-threatening bleeding and may be used to control active bleeding for surgery; however, they are ineffective as a treatment for ITP due to continued immune-mediated platelet destruction. This is not the appropriate choice for this case, as there is no evidence of significant active bleeding.

stem: A 42-year-old who has a known diagnosis of G6PD deficiency is admitted to the acute medical unit with jaundice. He has recently been unwell with a suspected urinary tract infection for which he had been prescribed nitrofurantoin. Bloods taken on admission are below; acute haemolysis is suspected. Hb 94 g/L (135-180) Platelets 210* 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 7.2*109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Reticulocytes 8.0% (0.2-2.0) Which underlying process will occur in response to the above presentation?
explanation:
Haptoglobin binds free haemoglobin
Haptoglobin binds free haemoglobin is correct following haemolysis, haptoglobin complexes with free haemoglobin, this complex can then bind to macrophage CD163 receptors allowing clearance and metabolism of the complex by the macrophage. This is an important pathway to avoid local toxicity from haemoglobin degradation products, such as free radicals. Accordingly, in cases of intravascular haemolysis, haptoglobin levels will quickly bind haemoglobin and their levels reduced upon testing.

Haemopexin binds free haemoglobin
Haemopexin binds free haemoglobin is incorrect. Haemopexin binds free haem, a product of free haemoglobin degradation, rather than haemoglobin itself.

Haptoglobin binds complexed haemoglobin
Haptoglobin binds complexed haemoglobin is incorrect. Haptoglobin is the protein that binds free haemoglobin to allow it to be scavenged by macrophages.

Haptoglobin binds free haem
Haptoglobin binds free heme is incorrect. As detailed above, haptoglobin binds free haemoglobin; failure of this process will cause the release of free haem.

Macrophages remove free haemoglobin
Macrophages remove free haemoglobin is incorrect. Macrophages are unable to remove free haemoglobin. They can only recognise and clear haemoglobin when it is bound to haptoglobin.

stem: A patient with testicular cancer is started on cisplatin therapy. Which of the following side-effects is most characteristically associated with cisplatin?
explanation:
Peripheral neuropathy
Cisplatin, a platinum-containing chemotherapeutic agent, is widely used in the treatment of numerous malignancies including testicular cancer. Its toxicity profile includes a well-characterised dose-dependent peripheral neuropathy. This presents as sensory symptoms beginning in the distal extremities and may be associated with motor weakness and autonomic dysfunction if severe. The pathophysiology involves damage to dorsal root ganglia neurons, leading to axonal degeneration.

Liver cirrhosis
Liver cirrhosis is not typically associated with cisplatin therapy. Liver toxicity can occur with some chemotherapy agents, but it's more commonly linked to drugs like methotrexate or azathioprine rather than cisplatin.

Alopecia
Alopecia, while a common side-effect of many chemotherapeutic agents, is not characteristically associated with cisplatin. It can occur but is less common compared to other drugs such as doxorubicin or cyclophosphamide.

Haemorrhagic cystitis
Haemorrhagic cystitis is a known complication of some chemotherapeutic agents, particularly cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide due to their toxic metabolite acrolein. It is not usually seen with cisplatin use.

Cardiomyopathy
Cardiomyopathy is also not typically associated with cisplatin therapy. Anthracyclines like doxorubicin are much more frequently implicated in chemotherapy-induced cardiotoxicity which can lead to cardiomyopathy.

stem: A 54-year-old man who has developed disseminated intravascular coagulation secondary to sepsis is reviewed. Twenty minutes ago he started to bleed per rectum. Blood products including packed red cells and fresh frozen plasma have been ordered. What is the single most important factor in determining whether cryoprecipitate should be given?
options: A high activated partial thromboplastin time
explanation:
A low fibrinogen level
A low fibrinogen level is the major criteria determining the use of cryoprecipitate in bleeding. Cryoprecipitate is a blood product that contains concentrated amounts of fibrinogen, factor VIII, and von Willebrand factor. It is primarily indicated for the treatment of hypofibrinogenaemia, which can occur in disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). In this case, the patient has developed DIC secondary to sepsis and has started bleeding per rectum. The administration of cryoprecipitate would be appropriate if the patient's fibrinogen level is low, as it would help replenish the depleted fibrinogen and promote clot formation.

A high prothrombin time
A high prothrombin time indicates a prolonged extrinsic pathway of coagulation, which may be due to deficiencies in factors II, V, VII or X. Although an elevated prothrombin time can be seen in DIC, it does not directly indicate a need for cryoprecipitate administration. Instead, fresh frozen plasma (FFP) would be more appropriate to address these deficiencies.

A high activated partial thromboplastin time
A high activated partial thromboplastin time suggests a prolonged intrinsic pathway of coagulation, which may result from deficiencies in factors II, V, VIII, IX or XI. Similar to a high prothrombin time, an elevated activated partial thromboplastin time does not necessarily indicate a need for cryoprecipitate; FFP would be more suitable for addressing these deficiencies.

A low platelet count
A low platelet count is common in DIC due to increased consumption and destruction of platelets. However, administering cryoprecipitate will not address this issue as it does not contain platelets. Instead, platelet transfusion should be considered to manage thrombocytopenia in this situation.

A low haemoglobin
A low haemoglobin level indicates anaemia, which may occur due to blood loss or haemolysis in DIC. While it is important to address a low haemoglobin level in this patient, cryoprecipitate is not the appropriate intervention as it does not contain red blood cells. Packed red blood cells (RBCs) should be transfused to manage anaemia and improve oxygen-carrying capacity.

stem: A 72-year-old man is referred to the haematology clinic complaining of lethargy and a rapidly growing lump in his right armpit. After a PET-CT and an excisional biopsy, he is diagnosed with diffuse large B cell lymphoma. He is due to start treatment with a monoclonal antibody that targets CD20. What should the patient be screened for prior to his first infusion?
explanation:
Hepatitis B
Patients starting rituximab should be screened for hepatitis B before starting treatment. The drug in question is rituximab which is a chimeric monoclonal antibody against CD20 which is expressed on B lymphocytes. Other antiCD20 monoclonal antibodies have been developed but rituximab is currently the standard one used for diffuse large B cell lymphoma. The correct answer is hepatitis B as it is the only disease that NICE states patients should be routinely screened for prior to starting rituximab. This is because of a risk of reactivation of the virus.

Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)
Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is not routinely tested for prior to starting rituximab, therefore this answer is incorrect. It is however linked to the development of Hodgkin's lymphoma, with around 40% of UK cases thought to be due to EBV.

Hepatitis C
Although there is also a theoretical risk of hepatitis C virus reactivation, research has not found evidence of this in practice. Therefore, routine screening is not currently advised by NICE. Interestingly, hepatitis C virus is itself linked to the development of some B cell lymphoproliferative disorders, such as cryoglobulinaemia, which rituximab is used to treat.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML)
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is screened for prior to commencing natalizumab (a monoclonal antibody that targets α4integrin) but is not routinely screened for in patients starting rituximab. The risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (caused by reactivation of the JC virus) is several times greater in patients receiving natalizumab than those receiving rituximab treatment. Natalizumab is used for the treatment of multiple sclerosis and Crohn's disease.

Tuberculosis
Whilst tuberculosis is screened for in patients starting infliximab (a monoclonal antibody targeting TNFα), routine screening is not currently advised by NICE for patients commencing rituximab treatment. Interestingly, the risk of tuberculosis reactivation is higher in infliximab than other anti-TNFα drugs such as etanercept, possibly due to infliximab binding more strongly to TNFα and also having a longer duration of action than etanercept.

stem: A 32-year-old woman attends the haematology clinic following a deep vein thrombosis in her left leg during a long-haul flight. She takes the combined oral contraceptive pill and has no other medical history. Her mother had a pulmonary embolism aged 45. Examination is unremarkable. Thrombophilia screening is performed. APTT ratio 0.9 (0.8-1.2) Protein C activity 98% (70-140%) Protein S activity 105% (60-140%) Antithrombin III activity 92% (80-120%) Lupus anticoagulant Negative - What is the most likely underlying thrombophilia?
explanation:
Factor V Leiden mutation
Factor V Leiden mutation results in activated protein C resistance. This is the most common inherited thrombophilia in the UK, affecting approximately 5% of the population. The key to this question is recognising that standard thrombophilia screening does not detect Factor V Leiden - it requires specific testing for activated protein C resistance or direct genetic testing for the Factor V Leiden mutation. The clinical scenario is highly suggestive: unprovoked VTE in a young woman with a family history of thromboembolism and an additional risk factor (combined oral contraceptive pill). All the standard tests shown are normal, which effectively excludes protein C, protein S, antithrombin III deficiencies, and antiphospholipid syndrome. Given the epidemiology and the normal screening results, Factor V Leiden is by far the most likely diagnosis and would require specific testing to confirm.

Prothrombin gene mutation
Prothrombin gene mutation is less likely. Whilst this is the second most common inherited thrombophilia (prevalence 1.5%), it also requires specific genetic testing and would not be detected by the standard screening shown. However, Factor V Leiden is more than three times more prevalent, making it statistically more likely in this clinical context with a positive family history.

Antiphospholipid syndrome
Antiphospholipid syndrome has been excluded by the negative lupus anticoagulant test. A complete antiphospholipid screen would also include anticardiolipin and anti-β2-glycoprotein I antibodies, but the negative lupus anticoagulant makes this diagnosis unlikely in the context of the other normal results.

Occult protein C deficiency
Occult protein C deficiency is implausible given the normal protein C activity of 98%. The combined oral contraceptive pill can lower protein C levels, so if anything, this result might underestimate her true baseline. A level within the normal range effectively excludes this diagnosis.

Occult antithrombin III deficiency
Occult antithrombin III deficiency is also implausible with a normal antithrombin III activity of 92%. Antithrombin levels are generally stable and not significantly affected by the oral contraceptive pill. The normal result makes this diagnosis very unlikely.

stem: What is the mechanism of action of cisplatin?
explanation:
Causes cross-linking in DNA
Cisplatin causes cross-linking in DNA. Cisplatin is a platinum-containing chemotherapeutic agent that forms covalent bonds with purine bases (particularly guanine) in DNA. This creates both intrastrand and interstrand cross-links, preventing DNA from unwinding and separating during cellular replication. This mechanism ultimately leads to apoptosis of rapidly dividing cells, making it particularly effective against various malignancies, especially testicular cancer, ovarian cancer, and certain lung cancers.

Stabilises DNA-topoisomerase II complex
Stabilises DNA-topoisomerase II complex is incorrect as this is the mechanism of action for different chemotherapeutic agents, specifically the topoisomerase inhibitors such as etoposide and doxorubicin. These drugs work by preventing the re-ligation of DNA strands after they have been cut by topoisomerase II, leading to cell death.

Inhibits ribonucleotide reductase
Inhibits ribonucleotide reductase is incorrect as this is the mechanism of action of hydroxyurea. This enzyme is responsible for converting ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides, which are essential for DNA synthesis. Hydroxyurea is commonly used in conditions such as sickle cell disease and certain myeloproliferative disorders.

Inhibits purine synthesis
Inhibits purine synthesis is incorrect as this is the mechanism of action of drugs such as methotrexate and mercaptopurine. These agents interfere with the de novo synthesis of purines, which are essential building blocks for DNA and RNA synthesis. These drugs are commonly used in conditions such as acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and rheumatoid arthritis.

Inhibits formation of microtubules
Inhibits formation of microtubules is incorrect as this is the mechanism of action of vinca alkaloids (such as vincristine and vinblastine) and taxanes (such as paclitaxel). These drugs interfere with microtubule formation or breakdown, preventing proper cell division during mitosis. They are commonly used in various malignancies including breast cancer and lymphomas.

stem: A 70-year-old woman presents with progressive symptoms of fatigue, weight loss and general aching, especially of the lower back. She has a past medical history of HIV with a suppressed viral load on treatment. She has been dependent on alcohol since her husband died 10 years ago and currently drinks a bottle of wine a day. Spinal X-rays identify multiple lytic lesions and blood tests confirm hypercalcaemia. As such a potential diagnosis of bone metastases is suspect and further investigations are planned including a PET and isotope bone scan. What is the most likely primary tumour site?
explanation:
Breast
Woman with bone metastases- most likely to originate in the breast Bone metastasis can unfortunately be the presenting issue in many patients with underlying cancer. Common features include bone pain, fatigue and signs and symptoms related to hypercalcaemia as calcium is released from bone structure. Breast cancer is one of the commonest malignancies in women and the commonest origin site for bone metastases.

Cervical
Cervical cancer remains in the top five commonest cancers in women worldwide however there has been a significant reduction in incidence achieved via human papillomavirus vaccination drives. Patients with uncontrolled HIV are three times more likely to develop cervical cancer however it still remains less common than breast cancer in patients with viral suppression. Bone metastasis in patients with cervical cancer is infrequent with the lungs and liver being the common sites for spread.

Liver
The most common risk factors associated with liver cancer are chronic infection with hepatitis B and C. Although this patient has a relatively higher risk of cancer due to excessive alcohol consumption most patients who develop liver cirrhosis do not progress to develop liver cancer. Finally, primary liver cancer has a relatively lower rate of metastasising when compared to breast cancer.

Lung
The incidence of lung cancer is strongly linked to tobacco smoke therefore its incidence is reduced in countries where smoking numbers are decreasing. Also, as smoking is less common in women worldwide, lung cancer is not commonly the primary site for bone metastasis unless a significant smoking history is provided.

Ovarian
Ovarian cancer although a common form of malignancy in women worldwide wide, has a lower rate of metastasising than other cancers such as breast cancer. Also, ovarian cancer generally metastases to the lungs, spleen and colon with spread to the bone being relatively rare.

stem: A 28-year-old woman has 24 hours of severe, colicky abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting. She reports multiple similar episodes in the past, often triggered by stress, during which she experiences symptoms of anxiety and depression. She has a pulse rate of 110 bpm, blood pressure of 150/93 mmHg, respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation at 98% on room air, and a temperature of 37.0ºC. She has epigastric tenderness without signs of peritonism and mild weakness in her lower limbs. A urine sample turns deep red after collection. Which investigation is most likely to aid in the diagnosis?
explanation:
Urinary porphobilinogen
Acute intermittent porphyria typically presents with abdominal, neurological and psychiatric symptoms. Urinary porphobilinogen is correct. Acute abdominal pain, neurologic features (such as lower limb weakness), and psychiatric symptoms (such as anxiety and depression) suggest acute intermittent porphyria (AIP). This patient’s urine turning deep red on standing is a classic feature of AIP due to the presence of urinary porphobilinogen undergoing reactions when exposed to air, forming reddish-brown, deep red pigments. During an acute attack of AIP, urinary porphobilinogen levels are significantly elevated, making this test the most specific and useful for diagnosing AIP during an acute attack.

Serum porphobilinogen
Serum porphobilinogen is incorrect as this is not routinely performed for AIP and would likely be less sensitive and specific for AIP during an acute attack. This is because, in AIP, porphobilinogen mainly accumulates in the urine, leading to significantly elevated levels during an acute attack. Hence, urinary tests are more reliable.

Serum uroporphyrin
Serum uroporphyrin is incorrect as this is associated with porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) instead, which leads to elevations due to defects in uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase. PCT typically presents with skin manifestations like photosensitivity and blistering, not with abdominal pain, psychiatric symptoms, and neurological features. In AIP, serum uroporphyrin is usually normal or only mildly elevated, making it an unsuitable test for diagnosing this condition.

Urinary delta-aminolaevulinic acid
Urinary delta-aminolaevulinic acid (ALA) is incorrect. While urinary ALA levels may also be raised in acute AIP attacks, it is less specific than urinary porphobilinogen. This is because elevated ALA can be seen in other conditions, such as lead poisoning, making it less strongly diagnostic. In AIP, urinary porphobilinogen is the most specific test and should be prioritised for diagnosis during an acute episode.

Urinary uroporphyrin
Urinary uroporphyrin is incorrect as elevated levels are instead associated with PCT. PCT tends to cause skin manifestations, such as photosensitivity and skin blistering instead of the acute abdominal, neurologic, and psychiatric features seen in this patient. In AIP, urinary uroporphyrin levels are usually normal or only mildly elevated, making it less useful in diagnosis.

stem: A 56-year-old woman presented to the breast clinic with a breast lump. On examination, there was a palpable irregular, 3 cm, non-tender lump in the left upper quadrant. She was subsequently diagnosed with ductal carcinoma in situ of the left breast. She was referred to the oncology team and commenced on anastrozole. What is the mechanism of action of the medication?
options: Binds to human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) receptors
explanation:
Reduces peripheral oestrogen synthesis
Anastrozole and letrozole are aromatase inhibitors that reduce peripheral oestrogen synthesis. In postmenopausal women, oestrogen is produced from peripheral tissues and lipids via the enzyme aromatase. Therefore, aromatase inhibitors such as anastrozole and letrozole which reduce peripheral oestrogen synthesis are frequently used to treat breast carcinoma in this group of patients.

Binds to human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) receptors
Trastuzumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds to HER2 receptors on the cancer cells, thereby suppressing the growth and proliferation of the tumour. It is effective in HER2-positive breast cancers.

Breaks down oestrogen receptors
Fulvestrant is a type of selective oestrogen receptor degrader that binds to and breaks down oestrogen receptors. Unlike tamoxifen, it does not have agonistic effects on the oestrogen receptor, instead, it leads to downregulation of the receptor.

Luteinising hormone-releasing hormone (LHRH) agonist
Goserelin is an LHRH agonist that suppresses oestrogen production by the ovaries. It can be used as adjuvant therapy in premenopausal women.

Oestrogen receptor antagonist
Tamoxifen is an antagonist (and a partial agonist) of oestrogen receptor. It is useful in oestrogen-receptor positive breast cancers and particularly in patients who have not gone through menopause.

stem: A 61-year-old man is referred by his family physician to a haematologist after he presented with a right-sided painless neck lump. The lump started small and has been slowly increasing in size. More recently a second lump has appeared which prompted the family physician to refer the patient. The patient has also been complaining of lethargy, night sweats and has lost significant weight. Thyroid function tests are normal and the patient does not have a significant family history. There is no recent travel or contact history. Biopsy of the nodes and cytogenetic analysis show a translocation causing increased B-cell lymphoma 2 (BCL-2) transcription which confirms the diagnosis. Unfortunately, the patient's condition cannot be treated with imatinib. Which of the following translocation does this patient have?
explanation:
t(14;18)
The t(14;18) translocation causes increased BCL-2 transcription and causes follicular lymphoma. This patient presented with the signs and symptoms suggestive of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. This is supported by the signs and symptoms of weight loss, night sweats, and painless lymphadenopathy. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is one class of lymphoma, with the other class being Hodgkin lymphoma. There are several types of Hodgkin lymphoma which are actually neoplasms of mature B cells, and very rarely of T cell origin. In this case, a cytogenetic analysis revealed a translocation causing increased BCL-2 transcription. This is associated with the t(14;18) translocation which causes follicular lymphoma.

t(11;14)
t(11;14) is associated with Mantle cell lymphoma, which is a type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. There is a translocation of cyclin D1 on chromosome 11 and heavy-chain Ig on chromosome 14. Mantle cell lymphoma is characteristic of being CD5 positive. It is known to be an aggressive tumor with late presentation and therefore poor prognosis.

t(15;17)
t(15;17) is associated with the acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) subtype of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). AML usually presents in patients above 65 years of age. The therapeutic importance of knowing the APL subtype is that it responds to all-trans retinoic acid (vitamin A).

t(12;15)
t(12;15) is associated with the development of breast cancer, more specifically secretory breast carcinoma. This type of breast cancer is known to be rare and the clinical outcome following is usually good.

t(11;22)
t(11;22) is a translocation which occurs in Ewing sarcoma. This is a malignant bone tumour which often occurs in individuals under 15 years of age. The disease is known to be very aggressive and is associated with the development of early metastases.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with confusion and lethargy. Her blood pressure is 90/70 mmHg, heart rate 110/min, and temperature 39.4ºC. On examination, she is pale, there is sternal tenderness with petechiae on her arms and legs and there is hepatosplenomegaly. Her cannula site is bleeding. Hb 78 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 30 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 25 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) PT 27 secs (10-14 secs) APTT 45 secs (25-35 secs) Fibrinogen 0.4 g/L (2 - 4) The patient is resuscitated with blood products and transferred to ICU. What chromosomal translocation is most likely to be identified on further testing?
explanation:
T15:17
Acute promyelocytic leukaemia - t(15;17) This patient presented with signs and symptoms suggestive of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). High white cell count, bony tenderness, and hepatosplenomegaly with DIC indicate acute leukaemia. The presence of DIC without any underlying cause in a young patient suggests acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APML). APML is associated with t (15:17) translocation involving the promyelocytic leukaemia (PML) gene and retinoic acid receptor alpha (RARA) gene, which gives rise to an abnormal retinoic acid receptor, inhibiting the differentiation of myeloblast. All-trans-retinoic acid is used for the treatment of APML which induces PML-RARA proteolysis and stimulates the differentiation of myeloblasts.

T11:14
T11:14 is a translocation between the cyclin D1 locus on chromosome 11 and the lg heavy chain locus on chromosome 14 and it is characteristic of mantle cell lymphoma.

T14:18
T14:18 is a translocation between the long arm of chromosome 18 near the BCL2 gene and the lg heavy chain gene on chromosome 14, leading to overexpression of the apoptosis inhibitor protein Bcl-2. It is commonly associated with follicular lymphoma.

T16:16
T16:16 are recurring chromosomal rearrangements commonly associated with the M4Eo subtype of acute myeloid leukaemia.

T9:22
T9:22 is a translocation of the ABL gene from chromosome 9 to 22 resulting in the formation of the Philadelphia chromosome, which encodes a protein with high tyrosine kinase activity that inhibits apoptosis and accelerates mitogenesis. It is a typical finding in chronic myeloid leukaemia.

stem: A 23-year-old patient is referred to the department of immunology with recurrent chest infections. He has no significant past medical history otherwise. The examination is unremarkable. Blood tests: IgA 0.1 g/L (0.6-5.00) IgG 3.1 g/L (6.0-16.6) IgM 0.24 g/L (0.53 - 2.47) B cells 250 cells/µL (100-500) What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Common variable immunodeficiency
Common variable immunodeficiency is correct. This typically presents with recurrent chest infections and hypogammaglobulinemia. Common variable immunodeficiency - low antibody levels, specifically in immunoglobulin types IgG, IgM and IgA. → recurrent chest and other infections

Chediak-Higashi syndrome
Chediak-Higashi syndrome is incorrect. This immune deficiency syndrome is characterized by partial albinism and peripheral neuropathy, which are not present here.

Severe combined immunodeficiency
Severe combined immunodeficiency is incorrect. This typically presents with recurrent viral and bacterial infections in the infant period and it is unlikely the patient would only present now for medical attention. It is also associated with low levels of immunoglobulins.

Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is incorrect. This is caused by a defect in the WASP gene. This causes recurrent bacterial infections but is also typically associated with eczema and thrombocytopenia, which are absent here.

X-linked congenital agammaglobulinaemia
X-linked congenital agammaglobulinaemia is incorrect. This can be difficult to differentiate clinically from CVID but typically B cells are normal in CVID and absent in this condition.

stem: A 22-year-old man attends the allergy clinic. Over the last 12 months, he has had recurrent attacks of swelling of his lips and tongue. These are often proceeded by a painful macular rash. At the clinic, what investigation is most appropriate to identify the diagnosis?
explanation:
C4
The clinical features are highly suggestive of hereditary angioedema. Low C2 and C4 levels are seen both during and even between attacks in this condition. However, serum C4 is the most reliable and widely used screening tool.

ANA
Although autoimmune conditions (such as systemic lupus erythematosus) can cause angioedema, there are no other clinical features in this case to suggest an autoimmune pathology.

C1-INH
Low levels of C1-INH occur during an attack, however, return to normal levels following recovery.

C2
Although low C2 levels are associated with hereditary angioedema, serum C4 is the most reliable and widely used screening tool.

Tryptase
Although anaphylaxis remains within the differential diagnosis, the presence of a painful macular rash makes this an exceedingly unlikely diagnosis.

stem: An 18-year-old male with known sickle cell is admitted to the haematology department with tiredness and yellowing of his eyes following a recent change in weather. You note his haemoglobin usually runs between 80-90g/L but an up to date blood test shows his Hb is now 53g/L. You suspect he is suffering from a haemolytic crisis. Which other blood parameter would you expect to be low in this patient's case?
explanation:
Haptoglobin
Haptoglobin binds to free haemoglobin. Patients with sickle cell disease usually have a degree of anaemia and are adapted to this. However, they can suffer from a haemolytic crisis where the Hb drops by 30-40g/L acutely giving them symptoms such as tiredness and jaundice. This can be triggered by infection, a change in the temperature (usually cold weather) and hypoxia to name a few. The accelerated break down of red blood cells releases haemoglobin which haptoglobin binds to, therefore reducing the levels of haptoglobin in the blood.

Reticulocytes
Reticulocytes are immature red blood cells and are released into the blood by the bone marrow in response to haemolysis and haemorrhage therefore their levels increase in a haemolytic crisis.

Conjugated bilirubin
High levels of conjugated bilirubin are due to conditions such as pancreatic cancer or biliary tree strictures, not haemolysis.

Unconjugated bilirubin
Haemolysis causes high levels of unconjugated bilirubin, not low levels.

Lactate dehydrogenase
Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is released from red cells as they break down, therefore, levels increase in a haemolytic crisis.

stem: A 48-year-old female presents to her family physician complaining of post-coital pain. She initially thought that this was related to her age but recently she has been feeling a constant dull pain in her pelvis. She also reports having a foul-smelling discharge from her vagina.
