stem: A 45-year-old woman has been diagnosed with breast cancer two months ago. Following mastectomy, she was started on a course of docetaxel by the oncology team. She is currently on her second cycle of treatment. What is the mechanism of action for this treatment?
options: It prevents microtubule depolymerisation and disassembly, decreasing free tubulin
It inhibits topoisomerase I which prevents relaxation of supercoiled DNA
It inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and thymidylate synthesis
It stabilises DNA-topoisomerase II complex which inhibits DNA & RNA synthesis
explanation:
It prevents microtubule depolymerisation and disassembly, decreasing free tubulin
Taxanes such as docetaxel - prevents microtubule depolymerisation & disassembly, decreasing free tubulin. Docetaxel belongs to the taxane family of medications. It is a chemotherapy agent designed to disrupt the normal function of microtubules by preventing microtubule depolymerisation and disassembly. This results in a reduction of free tubulin and thereby stopping cell division.

It inhibits topoisomerase I which prevents relaxation of supercoiled DNA
Topoisomerase inhibitors such as irinotecan work by inhibiting topoisomerase I which prevents relaxation of supercoiled DNA. This results in DNA damage and cell death.

It inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and thymidylate synthesis
Antimetabolites such as methotrexate work by inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase and thymidylate synthesis. This results in slowing and stopping DNA and protein synthesis that is necessary for normal cell cycle.

It causes cross-linking in DNA
Cisplatin is a cytotoxic drug that works by binding to DNA which results in cross-linking and inhibiting its replication.

It stabilises DNA-topoisomerase II complex which inhibits DNA & RNA synthesis
Doxorubicin is also a cytotoxic drug that works by stabilising the topoisomerase II complex. This stops the process of replication resulting in inhibition of DNA and RNA synthesis that is necessary for cell division.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presented with sudden onset gait ataxia, intention tremor and nystagmus. CT head demonstrated a 4cm left cerebellar haematoma. She is discussed with the local neurosurgical unit and urgently transferred for intervention. She is repatriated a week later for further rehabilitation. Routine blood tests are notable for a platelet count of 1,700 * 109/l. Initially, you attribute this to a post-surgical rise. However, on closer examination of her results you realise that on initial presentation her platelet count was 1,300 * 109/l. What gene mutation is likely to be discovered in this lady?
explanation:
JAK2
This lady has presented with a stroke at a young age, on a background of raised platelets. This is very suggestive of essential thrombocythaemia which is known to be a rare cause of stroke and is associated with a mutation in the JAK2 gene.

HFE
HFE mutation is seen in haemochromatosis.

CFTR
CFTR in cystic fibrosis.

WASP
WASP in Wiskott-Aldrich.

BCR-ABL
Mutations in BCR-ABL are associated with chronic myeloid leukaemia, and is known as the Philadelphia translocation.

stem: A 67-year-old man presents to the haematology clinic with fatigue and abnormal blood tests. He reports worsening lethargy over the preceding six months, as well as several episodes of profuse epistaxis requiring packing. More recently, he reports his vision becoming increasingly blurry, with a worsening headache. On clinical examination, you note hepatosplenomegaly and several rubbery lymph nodes in the anterior cervical chain. His blood tests are as follows: Hb 95 g/L Male: (135-180) Platelets 75 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 20 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) You order serum electrophoresis, which reveals an abnormal IgM peak. Which condition is this patient most likely to have?
explanation:
Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia
Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia (WM) is a B-cell lymphoma characterised by organomegaly, pancytopenia, and cold autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. The proliferative B-cells produce excessive IgM, and this forms a cornerstone of the diagnosis, alongside a biopsy. The combination of hyperviscosity symptoms (visual disturbance, headache), anaemia, thrombocytopaenia, raised white cell count, and organomegaly with lymphadenopathy with elevated IgM should prompt consideration of WM.

Multiple myeloma
Multiple myeloma is another B-cell tumour and can cause anaemia and thrombocytopaenia. However, the most common monoclonal band associated with it is IgA, followed by IgA and IgD. IgM-producing multiple myelomas are rare. Further, they are not associated with organomegaly, and most commonly feature bone pain. Other symptoms include those linked to hypercalcaemia and renal failure.

Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma (MALToma)
Mucosa-associated lymphatic tissue tumours (MALTomas) are another B-cell tumour. While any mucosal tissue can be affected, the most common location is the stomach, where it is strongly associated with Helicobacter pylori infection. There are no indications of this in the above case.

Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance
Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) is a condition characterised by a monoclonal gammopathy of less than 30g/L, as well as no CRAB symptoms (hypercalcaemia, renal failure, anaemia, bone pain). Since we have anaemia, this is not MGUS. It would also not explain the organomegaly.

Myelodysplasia
Myelodysplasia can cause anaemia, thrombocytopaenia, and organomegaly. However, it would not cause IgM paraproteinaemia or viscosity symptoms.

stem: A 65-year-old man comes for review. He has a history of small cell lung cancer and ischaemic heart disease. His cancer was diagnosed five months ago and he has recently completed a course of chemotherapy. From a cardiac point of view he had a myocardial infarction two years ago following which he had primary angioplasty with stent placement. He has had no angina since. For the past week he has become increasingly short-of-breath. This is worse at night and is associated with an occasional non-productive cough. He has also noticed that his wedding ring feels tight. Clinical examination is of his chest is unremarkable. He does however have distended neck veins and periorbital oedema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Superior vena cava obstruction
Superior vena cava obstruction is the correct answer in this case. The patient presents with classic signs of superior vena cava obstruction (SVCO), including increasing shortness of breath, distended neck veins, and periorbital oedema. The tight wedding ring suggests upper limb oedema, which is another characteristic finding. SVCO is a well-known complication of small cell lung cancer (SCLC), which commonly arises in the central airways and can directly invade or compress the superior vena cava. SCLC is the most common malignant cause of SVCO, accounting for approximately 22% of cases. The obstruction leads to impaired venous drainage from the head, neck, and upper limbs, resulting in the constellation of symptoms and signs described in this patient.

Heart failure secondary to chemotherapy
Heart failure secondary to chemotherapy is incorrect. While certain chemotherapeutic agents (particularly anthracyclines like doxorubicin) can cause cardiotoxicity leading to heart failure, the clinical picture does not fit with heart failure. The patient has distended neck veins, which could be seen in heart failure, but the periorbital oedema and tight wedding ring (suggesting upper limb oedema) are more consistent with SVCO. Additionally, heart failure typically presents with bilateral basal crackles on chest examination, which are not described here. The examination of his chest is noted to be unremarkable.

Tumour lysis syndrome
Tumour lysis syndrome is incorrect. Tumour lysis syndrome (TLS) is a metabolic emergency that occurs when large numbers of tumour cells are rapidly destroyed, releasing their contents into the bloodstream. It typically presents with hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia, and hyperuricaemia, leading to acute kidney injury, cardiac arrhythmias, seizures, or death. The clinical features described in this case (shortness of breath, distended neck veins, periorbital oedema) are not typical of TLS. Furthermore, TLS usually occurs during the initiation of chemotherapy rather than after completion.

Nephrotic syndrome secondary to chemotherapy
Nephrotic syndrome secondary to chemotherapy is incorrect. Nephrotic syndrome is characterised by heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, hyperlipidaemia, and oedema. While certain chemotherapeutic agents can cause renal damage leading to nephrotic syndrome, the distribution of oedema in nephrotic syndrome is typically generalised or dependent (affecting the lower limbs and sacrum when upright). The periorbital oedema could be seen in nephrotic syndrome, but the distended neck veins and predominant upper body oedema (tight wedding ring) are more consistent with SVCO.

Hypercalcaemia
Hypercalcaemia is incorrect. Hypercalcaemia is a common paraneoplastic syndrome in malignancy, particularly in lung cancer. However, the clinical features of hypercalcaemia typically include confusion, lethargy, constipation, polyuria, polydipsia, nausea, and vomiting, summarised by the phrase 'bones, stones, abdominal groans, and psychic moans.' The symptoms and signs described in this case (shortness of breath, distended neck veins, periorbital oedema, tight wedding ring) are not typical of hypercalcaemia and are more consistent with SVCO.

stem: A 39-year-old woman presents with a strange collection of symptoms over the past six months. She has been seen by multiple specialists, none of whom have been able to find a cause for her symptoms. Her symptoms include worsening headaches, memory loss, low mood, lethargy, abdominal pain causing paroxysms of intermittent generalised pain, nausea, an unusual taste in the mouth and paraesthesia in her extremities. She is irritable during your consultation and at times tearful complaining that no one is taking her seriously and confiding that her General Practitioner had referred her for counselling. Routine blood tests show: Hb 101g/L WBC 5.6 10*9/L Platelets 350 10*9/L MCV 77fL Na 136mmol/L K 4.3mmol/L Urea 18.2mmol/L Creatinine 408umol/L What is the likely cause of her symptoms?
explanation:
Lead poisoning
Abdominal pain, constipation, neuropsychiatric features, basophilic stippling → lead poisoning. It is important to keep lead poisoning in mind as a differential, particularly in someone for whom routine investigations are not providing an answer and who clearly has abnormal pathology (demonstrated by her kidney failure and microcytic anaemia). It can cause a varied and often non-specific array of symptoms. Some more 'classical' features include an unusual taste in the mouth and paraesthesia of the extremities. Questions may more obviously point to the route of exposure through industrial exposure or contact with lead-based products such as paint or contaminated water.

stem: A 52-year-old man with hypertension on ramipril is admitted for a lower respiratory tract infection and started on intravenous amoxicillin–clavulanate. Soon after treatment, he develops worsening breathlessness, widespread wheeze, and a non-specific skin eruption. His blood pressure is 80/50 mmHg, pulse 122 bpm, and oxygen saturation 88% on 100% oxygen. Immediate blood tests are taken: Hb 140 g/L (115 - 160) Platelets 154 * 10 9/L (150 - 400) WBC 8.3 * 10 9/L (4.0 - 11.0) Eosin 0.4 * 10 9/L (0.0 - 0.4) CRP 4 mg/L (< 5) Serum tryptase 9.8 µg/L (< 11.0) First-line treatment is given, and he improves. Which option is the best next test to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Arrange CT chest, followed by CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA)
Arrange skin prick test for amoxicillin–clavulanate
Measure total and specific serum IgE
explanation:
Repeat serum tryptase within 1-2 hours
Anaphylaxis - serum tryptase levels rise following an acute episode. Repeat serum tryptase within 1–2 hours is correct. This patient developed sudden hypotension, widespread wheezing, hypoxia, and a skin eruption shortly after starting intravenous amoxicillin–clavulanate, consistent with anaphylaxis. While the initial serum tryptase was normal (9.8 µg/L), this may have been taken too early. Tryptase peaks around 1–2 hours after mast cell degranulation, so repeating it at that time helps confirm mast cell activation. Hence, a single normal level does not rule out anaphylaxis. Hospital guidelines often recommend collecting one sample as soon as possible after the reaction, a second sample within 1–2 hours, and a third baseline sample 24 hours later or during follow-up. This allows comparison between acute and baseline tryptase levels to aid diagnosis.

Arrange CT chest, followed by CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA)
Arrange CT chest, followed by CTPA is incorrect. Although pulmonary embolism (PE) can cause acute breathlessness and hypoxia, this patient’s symptoms occurred soon after antibiotic administration and include wheeze and a skin eruption, which are not features of PE. These signs strongly suggest a systemic allergic reaction rather than a thromboembolic event. Elevated respiratory rate and hypoxia are better explained by bronchospasm due to anaphylaxis, making imaging less relevant at this stage.

Arrange skin prick test for amoxicillin–clavulanate
Arrange skin prick test for amoxicillin–clavulanate is incorrect as it is not suitable for confirming anaphylaxis during the acute phase. While skin prick testing may help identify the causative agent, it is performed weeks later in a specialist setting. This test does not confirm mast cell degranulation, which is needed now to support the diagnosis. This may be relevant instead if this patient had recovered from the acute event and required allergy testing to identify the trigger (e.g., amoxicillin–clavulanate), which would be done later under supervision, not during the perioperative crisis.

Measure C1-inhibitor levels
Measure C1-inhibitor levels is incorrect as C1-inhibitor deficiency causes bradykinin-mediated angioedema, not the IgE-mediated reaction seen here. While both can cause swelling and airway symptoms, this patient has skin eruption, wheezing, hypotension, and hypoxia immediately after treatment with amoxicillin–clavulanate, typical of anaphylaxis, not C1-inhibitor deficiency. This may be relevant instead if this patient had recurrent, non-pruritic facial or airway swelling without urticaria, bronchospasm, or hypotension, suggestive of hereditary or acquired angioedema, which is not seen in this acute perioperative context.

Measure total and specific serum IgE
Measure total and specific serum IgE is incorrect as these tests do not confirm acute mast cell activation. While they can help identify allergens in IgE-mediated hypersensitivity, they are not used to confirm anaphylaxis during or shortly after a reaction. This may be relevant instead if this patient had a history of atopy or suspected allergies outside the perioperative setting, presenting with recurrent urticaria or allergic symptoms, where total or specific IgE might support diagnosis, but this is not applicable in an acute event.

stem: A 66-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a rash over his lower limbs. He has recently recovered from an upper respiratory tract infection three weeks ago. He has no past medical history of note and is not taking any medications. On examination, you find widespread fine petechiae over the lower limbs and a large bruise over his right knee. The patient reports this occurred when he hit his knee whilst getting out of the car. There is no evidence of active bleeding. Observations are taken: Blood pressure 132/78 mmHg Heart rate 91 bpm Temperature 37.2ºC Saturations 95% on air Blood results show: Hb 121 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 8 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 4.5 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Na+ 140 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 3.9 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Urea 5.9 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 70 µmol/L (55 - 120) CRP 12 mg/L (< 5) Peripheral blood film True thrombocytopenia with no evidence of myelodysplasia What is the most appropriate initial of management for this patient?
explanation:
Oral prednisolone
Oral prednisolone is the correct answer in this circumstance due to the fact the patient is haemodynamically stable and the platelet count is below 30*109/L. The patient here has presented with a typical history of immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) which has been precipitated by a recent upper respiratory tract infection. The patient is haemodynamically stable without any significant active bleeding. Generally, asymptomatic patients do not require active treatment. However, where the platelet count falls below 30*109/L treatment is usually indicated due to the increased risk of bleeding once the platelet count falls to this level.

Intravenous immunoglobulin
Intravenous immunoglobulin is used in the treatment of ITP however it would not be indicated as a first-line treatment. IVIg is typically indicated where there has been a poor response to initial therapy or there are contraindications to steroid therapy.

Intravenous methylprednisolone
Intravenous methylprednisolone is used in the treatment of ITP however the patient in this circumstance is haemodynamically stable and can take medications orally. Initial therapy with oral prednisolone should be considered therefore in the first instance.

Observation
Observation would be considered if the platelet count was >30*109/L as a first-line treatment. However, in this circumstance the platelet count is 8*109/L and so the patient is at risk of severe bleeding with the current platelet count.

Pooled platelet transfusion
Pooled platelets are avoided in ITP unless the patient is suffering from life-threatening bleeding.

stem: An 18-year-old female presents to the emergency department with easy bruising, bleeding gums, and recurrent epistaxis. Additionally, she reports heavier than usual menstruation 2 weeks ago. She is otherwise well. On examination, there are areas of petechiae on the upper and lower limbs, evidence of dried blood in the nasal cavity, and small blood blisters on the tongue. There are no other abnormal findings. There is no evidence of active bleeding and she is haemodynamically stable. Investigations: Hb 110 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 34 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 8.0 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line therapy for this patient?
explanation:
Oral prednisolone
First-line treatment for ITP is oral prednisolone. The history provided above with significant thrombocytopaenia, normal white cell count and relatively normal haemoglobin in an otherwise well patient is consistent with a diagnosis of idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). The first-line treatment for ITP is 1-2mg/kg oral prednisolone.

Cyclophosphamide
Cyclophosphamide is an incorrect answer. Cyclophosphamide is not a first-line therapy for ITP. It can be used as a second-line therapy in the management of severe refractory ITP, although targeted monoclonal antibodies, like rituximab, have become a more preferred option.

Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG)
Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) is an incorrect answer. IVIG is used as a first-line therapy for patients with life-threatening haemorrhage or the potential for life-threatening haemorrhage. Typically this refers to patients with severe thrombocytopenia (<30x109/L) and evidence of a haemostatic defect (e.g. mucous membrane haemorrhage) or active bleeding. This patient has no evidence of active bleeding, her platelets are >30x109/L and she is haemodynamically stable.

Platelet transfusion
Platelet transfusion is an incorrect answer. Platelet transfusion is reserved for life-threatening bleeding in ITP. This patient has no evidence of active bleeding. Platelet transfusion in this scenario would result in rapid immune destruction of the platelets.

Splenectomy
Splenectomy is an incorrect answer. Splenectomy is not a first-line therapy for ITP. It is used as a second-line treatment for patients with steroid-refractory ITP.

stem: A patient is diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia after presenting with lethargy and easy bruising. Which one of the following is a marker of a bad prognosis in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia?
explanation:
Philadelphia chromosome positive
The Philadelphia chromosome is a specific genetic abnormality in chromosome 22 of leukaemia cancer cells. It results from a reciprocal translocation between chromosome 9 and 22, which leads to the formation of BCR-ABL fusion gene that encodes for a tyrosine kinase protein with unregulated activity. This protein plays a crucial role in cell proliferation and survival, contributing to the pathogenesis of leukaemia. The presence of this Philadelphia chromosome is associated with a worse prognosis in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL), as it often leads to resistance against traditional chemotherapy agents.

Pre-B phenotype
Pre-B phenotype is not associated with poor prognosis in ALL. In fact, pre-B-cell ALL represents the most common subtype of ALL and usually has a favourable outcome, especially when treated according to current treatment protocols.

Presentation in childhood
Presentation in childhood does not indicate a poor prognosis but instead is associated with better outcomes compared to adult ALL. Children generally respond better to chemotherapy than adults and have higher cure rates.

Initial white cell count of 18 * 109/l
An Initial white cell count of 18 * 109/l also does not signify a bad prognosis. High white blood cell count at diagnosis (>30 * 109/l in children or >100 * 109/l in adults) can be associated with poorer outcomes, but an initial count of 18 falls well within normal range.

Female sex
Female sex does not correlate with poorer outcomes in ALL. There are no significant differences between sexes regarding response to treatment or overall survival rates; both males and females have similar prognoses when other factors are accounted for.

stem: An 80-year-old woman is seen in GP due to weight loss, night sweats and fatigue over the preceding weeks. On examination, she is pale and palpation of her abdomen reveals hepatosplenomegaly. She has a past medical history of polycythaemia vera. A full blood count reveals pancytopaenia. Blood film shows a characteristic finding associated with the new condition. What characteristic finding on blood film is most associated with this patient's new condition?
explanation:
Tear drop poikilocytes
Myelofibrosis is associated with 'tear drop' poikilocytes on blood film. The condition being described is myelofibrosis. This patient is at particular risk of developing myelofibrosis: approximately 6-10% of patients with polycythaemia vera develop myelofibrosis due to marrow exhaustion. Myelofibrosis is a myeloproliferative disorder thought to be caused by hyperplasia of abnormal megakaryocytes. Bone marrow does not produce the normal range of mature cells, leading to anaemia and eventually pancytopaenia (note early in the disease high WBC and platelet counts are often seen). Haematopoiesis develops in the liver and spleen resulting in organomegaly. The characteristic blood film finding in myelofibrosis is tear drop poikilocytes. This is a result of extramedullary haematopoiesis (mainly splenic), producing aberrantly shaped red blood cells.

Heinz bodies
Heinz bodies are associated with G6PD deficiency. Heinz bodies are formed through oxidative damage to haemoglobin molecules, usually through inherited mutations or drug administration. Heinz body anaemia can occur as these damaged cells are removed from the circulation by the spleen. In this scenario, the patient has anaemia but this is due to marrow failure; there is no mention of any conditions in the stem that suggest the presence of Heinz bodies.

Pencil poikilocytes
Pencil poikilocytes are associated with iron-deficiency anaemia. While the patient in this scenario has anaemia, this is a result of marrow failure rather than iron deficiency so they are unlikely to have pencil poikilocytes.

Schistocytes
Schistocytes are associated with haemolytic anaemias. They are fragmented red blood cells, formed through mechanical damage in the circulation; the most common causes are mechanical heart valves, haemolytic anaemias and microangiopathic diseases such as DIC. There is no mention that this patient has a mechanical heart valve. While the patient has hepatosplenomegaly, it is unlikely she has haemolytic anaemia given she is not jaundiced.

Spherocytes
Spherocytes are associated with hereditary spherocytosis and immunemediated haemolytic anaemias. Spherocytes are broken down by the spleen, leading to splenomegaly and anaemia. While this patient has splenomegaly, this is secondary to extramedullary haematopoiesis rather than excessive splenic consumption.

stem: A 38-year-old female patient presents to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting. She also reports reduced sensation in the bilateral lower limb extremities. She appears highly agitated and labile in mood. Her partner reports that this has happened about 6 times before and various suspected diagnoses were made for these past episodes but no definite diagnosis was ever made. She reports that her mother also gets such episodes. These past suspected diagnoses include acute appendicitis, renal calculi, acute intestinal obstruction. They were all found to be negative. What is the likely diagnosis to account for this clinical presentation?
explanation:
Acute intermittent porphyria
Acute intermittent porphyria typically presents with abdominal, neurological and psychiatric symptoms. AIP is more likely given the family history.

Porphyria cutanea tarda
Porphyria cutanea tarda presents with photosensitive bullae.

Lead poisoning
Lead poisoning is possible to account for this presentation but it doesn't account for the family history.

Neurotic disorder
Neurotic disorder may be possible but physical causes need to be ruled out before considering a psychiatric diagnosis.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis doesn't usually present with gastrointestinal symptoms.

stem: A 40-year-old male patient is admitted with recurrent pancreatitis. A CT scan reveals no pancreatic mass, but evidence of widespread lymphadenopathy. Dedicated liver imaging reveals a stricture in the common bile duct but no stones. He also has a history of parotiditis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
IgG4 disease
IgG4-related disease has been described in virtually every organ system: the biliary tree, salivary glands, periorbital tissues, kidneys, lungs, lymph nodes, meninges, aorta, breast, prostate, thyroid, pericardium, and skin. The histopathological features are similar across organs, regardless of the site. IgG4-related disease is analogous to sarcoidosis, in which diverse organ manifestations are linked by similar histopathological characteristics. Raised concentrations of IgG4 in tissue and serum can be helpful in diagnosing IgG4 disease, but neither is a specific diagnostic marker.

stem: A 56 year old man is treated with doxorubicin for transition cell carcinoma of the bladder. Which one of the following adverse effects is most characteristically associated with this drug?
explanation:
Cardiomyopathy
Doxorubicin, an anthracycline, is most characteristically associated with cardiotoxicity, which can manifest as cardiomyopathy. The mechanism of this adverse effect involves the generation of free radicals and oxidative stress that lead to myocardial damage. Cardiotoxicity may present either acutely during treatment, or chronically months to years after cessation of therapy. It is important to monitor patients receiving doxorubicin for signs of heart failure.

Ototoxicity
Ototoxicity is incorrect because it's not typically associated with doxorubicin. This side effect is more commonly linked with aminoglycosides and platinum-based chemotherapy agents such as cisplatin.

Pulmonary fibrosis
Pulmonary fibrosis is also incorrect as it's not a characteristic adverse effect of doxorubicin. Pulmonary fibrosis is more commonly seen with drugs like bleomycin and amiodarone.

Peripheral neuropathy
Peripheral neuropathy while being a common side effect of many chemotherapeutic agents, particularly the taxanes and platinum-based drugs, it's not significantly associated with doxorubicin use.

Haemorrhagic cystitis
Haemorrhagic cystitis is incorrect as well. This condition is specifically linked to cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide usage, rather than doxorubicin. It occurs due to toxic metabolites irritating the bladder lining leading to bleeding from the urinary tract.

stem: Which one of the following is least associated with eosinophilia?
explanation:
Histoplasmosis
The correct answer is Histoplasmosis. Histoplasmosis is a fungal infection caused by the Histoplasma capsulatum organism. It primarily affects the lungs and does not typically cause eosinophilia, which is an increase in the number of eosinophils, a type of white blood cell, in the body. Eosinophilia is usually associated with allergic reactions or parasitic infections, neither of which are typical features of histoplasmosis.

Churg-Strauss syndrome
Churg-Strauss syndrome, now more commonly known as eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), is incorrect because it is strongly associated with eosinophilia. EGPA is a rare autoimmune condition characterised by asthma, lung infiltrates and systemic vasculitis. The disease frequently presents with marked peripheral blood and tissue eosinophilia.

Nematode infection
Nematode infection is also incorrect as it's well known to be associated with eosinophilia. Nematodes or roundworms can cause a wide range of diseases in humans, many of which result in significant peripheral eosinophilia. This occurs as part of the host immune response to these parasites.

Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis
Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) is incorrect because this condition too has a strong association with eosinophilia. ABPA represents an allergic reaction to the fungus Aspergillus fumigatus, leading to inflammation and damage to the airways. Eosinophils play a key role in allergy-mediated responses; hence patients with ABPA often have high levels of these cells.

Asthma
Asthma is another incorrect answer because it's commonly associated with eosinophilia, especially in its more severe forms. In fact, elevated eosinophil counts in sputum or peripheral blood can be used as one marker for asthma severity and control according to UK guidelines such as those from British Thoracic Society (BTS) and Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network (SIGN).

stem: A 27-year-old woman with a background of systemic lupus erythematosus has progressed to end-stage renal failure following a period of declining renal function. An urgent renal biopsy was performed which confirmed the presence of lupus nephritis. Her case was discussed in the MDT meeting and she was commenced on various drug treatments to help suppress the immune system. A few days into the course of her treatment she developed gross macroscopic haematuria which the team felt was likely to have been caused by one of the new medications. Mesna was given to treat this side effect. What is the mechanism of action of the offending medication in this case?
options: Increases lysosomal pH in antigen-presenting cells
explanation:
Cross-linking in DNA
Cyclophosphamide - causes cross-linking in DNA Cross-linking in DNA is the mechanism by which cyclophosphamide acts as a chemotherapy agent and is used to suppress the immune system in various conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus, nephrotic syndrome, granulomatosis with polyangiitis and severe rheumatoid arthritis. It has mainly important side effects to be aware of one of which is haemorrhagic cystitis which can result in dysuria and gross macroscopic haematuria. This can be prevented with adequate fluid intake, avoiding night-time dosing and the use of mesna.

Degrades preformed DNA
Degrading performed DNA is a mechanism by which bleomycin works to treat cancers and can cause lung fibrosis as an adverse effect.

Increases lysosomal pH in antigen-presenting cells
Increasing lysosomal pH in antigen-presenting cells is how hydroxychloroquine works as a disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD) used in rheumatoid arthritis and lupus. Hydroxychloroquine has side effects of retinopathy and ventricular arrhythmias.

Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase
Dihydrofolate reductase inhibitors e.g. methotrexate is chemotherapy and immunosuppressive agent which inhibits. They are used to treat cancers and autoimmune diseases.

stem: A 31-year-old woman with known sickle cell disease presents to her GP feeling acutely lethargic. She has also noticed palpitations and shortness of breath on exertion. She has previously been fit and well. However, her daughter has been unwell over the past few days with fevers, malaise and a facial rash. Blood test results 3 months ago: Hb 116 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 178 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 6.3 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Blood test results today: Hb 71 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 110 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 4.1 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Reticulocytes 0.1 % (0.5 - 1.5) What is the most likely complication which has occurred here?
explanation:
Aplastic crisis
Aplastic crises in sickle cell disease are associated with a sudden drop in haemoglobin. The correct answer here is aplastic crisis in sickle cell disease. There are multiple clues to this, including the symptoms of anaemia, the exposure to parvovirus B-19 (which is the most common trigger) and the drop in haemoglobin with a low reticulocyte count. This implies acute bone marrow failure.

Acute chest syndrome
Acute chest syndrome is an acute respiratory complication of sickle cell disease. However, that would not explain the blood results.

Acute splenic sequestration
Haemolytic crisis and acute splenic sequestration would also cause a sudden drop in haemoglobin levels in sickle cell patients. However, in these conditions, you would expect a raised reticulocyte count, given that the problem is with red blood cell survival rather than red blood cell production.

Community acquired pneumonia
Community-acquired pneumonia would cause respiratory symptoms but would not account for the blood results noted here.

Haemolytic crisis
Haemolytic crisis and acute splenic sequestration would also cause a sudden drop in haemoglobin levels in sickle cell patients. However, in these conditions, you would expect a raised reticulocyte count, given that the problem is with red blood cell survival rather than red blood cell production.

stem: A 18-year-old man who is known to have hereditary spherocytosis is admitted to hospital with lethargy. Admission bloods show the following: Hb 47 g/dL Male: (135-180) Retics 0.3% 0.5-1.5% What is the most likely explanation for these findings?
explanation:
Parvovirus infection
The correct answer is Parvovirus infection. Hereditary spherocytosis (HS) is a genetic condition characterised by abnormally shaped red blood cells that are destroyed prematurely in the spleen. The combination of severe anaemia with a low reticulocyte count (reticulocytopenia) in a patient with HS is highly suggestive of a parvovirus B19 infection causing an aplastic crisis. Parvovirus B19 temporarily stops red blood cell production in the bone marrow by infecting erythroid precursor cells. This is particularly significant in patients with HS who already have a shortened red cell survival.

Haemolytic crisis
Haemolytic crisis would present with severe anaemia but would show an elevated reticulocyte count (reticulocytosis) as the bone marrow attempts to compensate for increased red cell destruction. The low reticulocyte count in this case rules out a haemolytic crisis.

Recent ciprofloxacin therapy
Recent ciprofloxacin therapy is not associated with bone marrow suppression or aplastic crisis. While some antibiotics can cause haemolysis in susceptible individuals, ciprofloxacin is not typically associated with this effect.

Sequestration crises
Sequestration crises occur when red blood cells become trapped in the spleen, causing sudden splenic enlargement and anaemia. However, this would also show an elevated reticulocyte count as the bone marrow would respond to the anaemia.

Angiodysplastic bowel lesions
Angiodysplastic bowel lesions could cause chronic blood loss anaemia but would not explain the low reticulocyte count. In chronic blood loss, the reticulocyte count would be elevated as the bone marrow responds to the anaemia.

stem: A 53-year-old gentleman of Mediterranean descent presented to the GP surgery with increased fatigue, jaundice and abdominal discomfort. There is no history of rigor, vomiting or any bowel symptoms. He has a background of type 2 diabetes, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, hypertension, glucose-6-phosphate deficiency and hyperlipidaemia. His regular medications include lansoprazole, ramipril, metformin, simvastatin and glimepiride. He drinks approximately 10 units of alcohol per week. Examination shows mild scleral icterus, splenomegaly and mild abdominal tenderness in the left upper quadrant. His recent blood results are as follow: Hb 122g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 180* 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 6.2* 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Bilirubin 34 µmol/L (3 - 17) ALP 90u/L (30 - 100) ALT 35u/L (3 - 40) γGT 60 u/L (8 - 60) Albumin 36 g/L (35 - 50) Blood film shows bite cells and blister cells. Which medication is the most likely to be responsible for his symptom?
explanation:
Glimepiride
G6PD deficiency: sulph- drugs: sulphonamides, sulphasalazine and sulfonylureas can trigger haemolysis. The correct answer is glimepiride. It belongs to the sulphonylurea class of diabetes medicine. It is used in the treatment of type 2 diabetes. It can trigger haemolysis in patients with G6PD deficiency. The finding of mild anaemia, raised bilirubin and the presence of bite cells and blister cells on blood film are suggestive of haemolytic anaemia.

Ramipril
Ramipril is not known to cause haemolytic anaemia.

Metformin
Metformin is not known to cause haemolytic anaemia.

Simvastatin
Simvastatin can cause jaundice by inducing hepatitis. Normal alanine transaminase and alkaline phosphatase makes this unlikely.

Lansoprazole
Lansoprazole is not known to cause haemolytic anaemia.

stem: An 18-year-old is due to start chemotherapy for a new diagnosis of testicular cancer. He is being counselled on a platinum-based cytotoxic medication which works by causing damage to purine bases on DNA. It is explained to him that certain baseline tests may be done before treatment to help identify adverse reactions to the chemotherapy. What is the most appropriate test to identify a potential adverse reaction to this medication?
explanation:
Audiometric testing
Cisplatin may cause ototoxicity. Audiometric testing is correct. Ototoxicity is an uncommon but important adverse effect of cisplatin in both paediatric and adult patients. Cisplatin is a platinum-based anti-neoplastic medication used in the treatment of testicular cancer. It binds to the purine base guanine, interfering with DNA repair and inhibiting its replication. For some patients, especially children or those with prior hearing loss, audiometric testing may be done before and after administration. The degree of toxicity is dose-related.

CT chest
CT chest is incorrect. This would identify lung fibrosis which is more typically associated with methotrexate and bleomycin. Regardless, CT chest would not be a suitable baseline test to perform prior to starting methotrexate or bleomycin.

Gait analysis
Gait analysis is incorrect. This would detect ataxia which is more commonly associated with cytarabine which is normally used in the treatment of acute myeloid leukaemia. Cisplatin does not commonly cause ataxia.

Transthoracic echocardiogram
Transthoracic echocardiogram is incorrect. This would identify cardiomyopathies which are typically associated with doxorubicin. Doxorubicin typically causes a dilated cardiomyopathy and an echocardiogram may be performed prior to starting treatment.

Upper GI endoscopy
Upper GI endoscopy is incorrect. This would identify mucositis (inflammation and erosion of the mucosa of the GI tract). Mucositis is typically associated with fluorouracil (5FU) which is used for solid tumours and basal skin cancer, but not commonly testicular cancer.

stem: A 52-year-old woman presents with fever, sweats and persistent dyspepsia despite omeprazole. She has also lost 5kg in weight over the last 1 year. Prior to this she is normally fit and well with no other past medical or drug history. She works as a bus driver and her only recent foreign travel was to Ibiza on holiday. She undergoes an endoscopy which reveals a tumour in the antrum of the stomach. Which of the following is most likely to have been causative?
explanation:
Helicobacter pylori
Helicobacter pylori infection can lead to gastric lymphoma (MALT). These are typically arise in the antrum of the stomach and can present with systemic features such as fevers and night sweats.

Epstein Barr virus
Epstein Barr Virus (EBV) predisposes to nasopharyngeal cancer and Hodgkin's lymphoma.

Coeliac disease
While coeliac disease can predispose to gastrointestinal (GI) tumours, this is rare. Furthermore, coeliac is associated with enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma, a disease of the small intestine.

Schistosoma haematobium
Schistosoma haematobium predisposes to bladder tumours.

Human T-lymphotropic virus 1
HTLV1 predisposes to adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma.

stem: A 72-year-old man is reviewed in a pre-operative assessment clinic. He feels well, with no weight loss or night sweats. On examination, he has a few small, mobile, non-tender cervical lymph nodes. A routine full blood count is performed. WBC 45.0 x 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Lymphocytes 38.5 x 109/L (1.0 - 4.0) Hb 128 g/L (135 - 180) Platelets 145 x 109/L (150 - 400) What is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
options: CT scan of neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis
explanation:
Immunophenotyping of peripheral blood
The patient presents with a marked, isolated lymphocytosis (38.5 x 109/L) found incidentally. In an older adult, this is highly suggestive of Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia (CLL). The definitive diagnosis of CLL is made by identifying a clonal population of B-lymphocytes in the peripheral blood. Immunophenotyping, using flow cytometry, is the gold-standard investigation for this. It analyses cell surface markers (CD antigens) to identify the characteristic CLL phenotype: a monoclonal B-cell population that co-expresses CD5 and CD23, along with pan B-cell markers such as CD19 and CD20. According to UK guidelines, a diagnosis can be confidently made with a persistent monoclonal B-cell count of >5 x 109/L in the peripheral blood, making more invasive tests like a bone marrow biopsy unnecessary for initial diagnosis in most cases.

Bone marrow aspirate and trephine
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine is not the first-line investigation for diagnosing CLL. While it is an important tool in the management of CLL, it is typically reserved for specific indications. These include pretreatment assessment to establish a baseline of marrow infiltration, investigating unexplained or worsening cytopenias (to distinguish between marrow failure and autoimmune causes), and for prognostic purposes through cytogenetic analysis (e.g., FISH for del17p). In this asymptomatic patient with a new presentation, the diagnosis can and should be confirmed non-invasively using peripheral blood first.

CT scan of neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis
CT scan of neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis is a staging investigation, not a diagnostic one. Once a diagnosis of CLL is confirmed, a CT scan is used to assess the extent of lymphadenopathy and organomegaly (hepatosplenomegaly). This information is used to determine the clinical stage (e.g., Binet or Rai staging), which is essential for prognostication and making decisions about when to initiate treatment. However, it plays no role in establishing the initial histological or cytological diagnosis.

Excisional lymph node biopsy
Excisional lymph node biopsy would be the primary investigation for a patient presenting with significant lymphadenopathy in the absence of a peripheral lymphocytosis, where a diagnosis of lymphoma (e.g., small lymphocytic lymphoma, SLL) is suspected. SLL is considered the same disease as CLL, but primarily located in the lymph nodes. Given the very high lymphocyte count in this patient's blood, the disease is clearly leukaemic, and the peripheral blood is the most appropriate and least invasive tissue to sample for diagnosis. A biopsy might be considered later if there was a clinical suspicion of transformation to a high-grade lymphoma (Richter's transformation), which is not suggested by this scenario.

Serum protein electrophoresis
Serum protein electrophoresis is used to detect and quantify monoclonal proteins (paraproteins) in the blood. While a small monoclonal gammopathy can be present in up to 20% of patients with CLL, and hypogammaglobulinaemia is also a common finding, this test does not diagnose the underlying leukaemia. It provides information about the immune dysregulation associated with the disease but does not identify the clonal lymphocytes themselves. It is part of the general work-up for a lymphoproliferative disorder but is not the primary diagnostic test.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is admitted to the acute medical unit with an acute history of diffuse abdominal pain and constipation. She also reports burning pains in her legs associated with hyperaesthesia. A psychiatric review has also been requested as the patient is experiencing auditory hallucinations, with no history of mental health diagnoses. On examination she is tachycardia and proximal muscle weakness is also noted. She has no significant past medical history, although has recently changed her diet in a bid to lose weight. Which single investigation is likely to be diagnostic?
explanation:
Urine porphobilinogen
In acute intermittent porphyria, urinary porphobilinogen is typically raised. This patient is presenting with classic features of acute intermittent porphyria. Abdominal pain and constipation are the most common symptoms, however neuropathic pain, proximal muscle weakness and neuropsychiatric symptoms can also manifest. An elevated urine porphobilinogen is diagnostic for the condition, and ideally should be tested from a single volume urine sample.

Delta-aminolevulinic acid
Delta-aminolevulinic acid is widely thought to be the agent behind the pain experienced in porphyria attacks. Although it is likely to be elevated, it is not as sensitive as porphobilinogen in diagnosing the condition.

Faecal total porphyrins
Faecal total porphyrins are indicated in patients with increased porphobilinogen. This aids the differentiation of acute intermittent porphyrias from hereditary coproporphyria and variegate porphyria; faecal porphyrins would be significantly elevated in the latter.

Plasma total porphyrins
Plasma total porphyrins can be normal or elevated in acute intermittent porphyria. However, levels will be elevated in variegate porphyria, hence it is a useful investigation in a porphyria work up.

Urine total porphyrins
Urine total porphyrins will be elevated in acute intermittent porphyria, however, it is a less sensitive test compared to urobilinogen.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath. She has no history of recent surgery, immobilisation or prolonged travel. She has a past medical history of a right sided calf deep vein thrombosis (DVT) two years previously. She is not taking any medications, including the combined oral contraceptive pill. Her family history is significant for an unprovoked DVT in her mother. On examination, she is tachycardic and tachypnoeic. Her chest is clear and heart sounds are normal. Her calves are both soft and non-tender. She has a normal body mass index. ECG demonstrates sinus tachycardia. Her blood results are: Hb 140 g/L Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 250 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 6.2 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Na+ 140 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 4.0 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Urea 5.5 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 95 µmol/L (55 - 120) CRP <5 mg/L (< 5) Prothrombin time (PT) 12 secs (10-14 secs) Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) 30 secs (25-35 secs) Fibrinogen 3.0 g/L (2 - 4) D-Dimer 950 ng/mL (< 400) CT pulmonary angiogram demonstrated bilateral pulmonary emboli and she was commenced on anticoagulation. Which of the following best describes the most likely underlying pathology?
explanation:
Resistance to protein C
Activated protein C resistance (Factor V Leiden) is the most common inherited thrombophilia. Resistance to protein C occurs in Factor V Leiden, which is the correct answer as it is the most common inherited thrombophilia. A history of recurrent unprovoked venous thromboembolism should raise the concern for an inherited thrombophilia. Missense mutation in the Factor V gene makes factor V ten times less sensitive to inactivation by activated protein C, leading to thrombophilia.

Deficiency of protein C
Mutations in the gene encoding natural anticoagulants antithrombin III, protein C and protein S can lead to thrombophilia but these are less common. These mutations can be either cause a deficiency or loss of function.

Deficiency of protein S
Mutations in the gene encoding natural anticoagulants antithrombin III, protein C and protein S can lead to thrombophilia but these are less common. These mutations can be either cause a deficiency or loss of function.

Mutation in prothrombin gene
Prothrombin G20210A (prothrombin gene mutation) is the second most common inherited cause of thrombophilia (UpToDate).

Resistance to protein S
Mutations in the gene encoding natural anticoagulants antithrombin III, protein C and protein S can lead to thrombophilia but these are less common. These mutations can be either cause a deficiency or loss of function.

stem: Which one of the following would most suggest a leukaemoid reaction rather than chronic myeloid leukaemia?
options: A low leucocyte alkaline phosphatase score
Dohle bodies in the white cells
explanation:
Dohle bodies in the white cells
Dohle bodies are blue-grey, oval cytoplasmic inclusions found in neutrophils during toxic states or infections. They are characteristic of a leukaemoid reaction, which is a reactive process mimicking leukaemia, typically occurring in response to severe infection, inflammation, or malignancy. Their presence strongly suggests a reactive process rather than a primary haematological malignancy like chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML).

Raised packed cell volume
Raised packed cell volume is not a reliable distinguishing feature between leukaemoid reaction and CML. While it can occur in both conditions, it's not specifically characteristic of either. In CML, the packed cell volume may actually be low due to bone marrow displacement.

Right shift of neutrophils
Right shift of neutrophils (increased mature forms) can occur in both conditions and is not discriminatory. In fact, CML often shows a full spectrum of myeloid cells from blast cells to mature neutrophils, while a leukaemoid reaction typically shows predominantly mature forms.

A low leucocyte alkaline phosphatase score
A low leucocyte alkaline phosphatase score is actually more suggestive of CML rather than a leukaemoid reaction. In CML, the LAP score is characteristically low, while in a leukaemoid reaction it is typically normal or elevated, making this answer incorrect.

Positive osmotic fragility test
Positive osmotic fragility test is not particularly relevant to distinguishing between these conditions. This test is primarily used to diagnose hereditary spherocytosis and other red cell membrane disorders, and does not help differentiate between leukaemoid reaction and CML.

stem: A patient develops methaemoglobinaemia after being prescribed isosorbide mononitrate. Which substance is most likely to be depleted?
explanation:
NADH
The correct answer is NADH. Methaemoglobinaemia results from the oxidation of the iron in haemoglobin to its ferric state, which reduces the molecule's ability to carry oxygen. NADH is a crucial cofactor for methaemoglobin reduction back to haemoglobin via cytochrome b5 reductase. Therefore, depletion of NADH could potentially exacerbate methaemoglobinaemia by impairing this reduction process.

Pyruvate kinase
Pyruvate kinase is an enzyme involved in glycolysis, converting phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate and generating ATP. It does not directly involve in the metabolism or detoxification of nitric oxide (NO) derivatives like isosorbide mononitrate, so it would not be depleted in this situation.

Hyponitrite reductase
Hyponitrite reductase does not exist and seems to be a confusion with nitrite reductase, which converts nitrites into ammonia. This enzyme is found mainly in bacteria and plants but not in humans.

Pyridoxine 5-dehydrogenase
Pyridoxine 5-dehydrogenase, also known as Pyridoxal kinase, phosphorylates vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) into its active form pyridoxal phosphate (PLP). PLP acts as a coenzyme for many reactions but does not directly involve in NO metabolism or methaemoglobin reduction.

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency can cause haemolytic anaemia when patients are exposed to certain medications or infections due to increased oxidative stress on red blood cells. However, G6PD does not play a direct role in reducing methaemoglobin back to haemoglobin, hence it would not be depleted following the administration of isosorbide mononitrate leading to methaemoglobinaemia.

stem: A 4-year-old girl with sickle cell anaemia presents with abdominal pain. On examination, she is noted to have splenomegaly and is clinically anaemic. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Sequestration crisis
During a sequestration crisis, the sickle cells cause the spleen to become grossly enlarged causing the abdominal pain as present in this case. This is more common in early childhood as repeated sequestration and infarction of the spleen during childhood gradually results in an autosplenectomy. A sequestration crisis may result in severe anaemia, marked pallor and cardiovascular collapse due to loss of effective circulating volume.

stem: A 60-year-old man receives multiple units of packed red blood cells whilst being treated for a bleeding peptic ulcer. He has a history of HIV and is non-compliant with his antiretroviral treatment. His blood tests are normal upon discharge. He presents to the emergency department a week later with a macular erythematous rash, jaundice, fever and diarrhoea. On examination, he is tachypnoeic and there is hepatomegaly. Hb 75 g/L Male: (135-180) Platelets 23 * 10 9/L (150 - 400) WBC 2.4 * 10 9/L (4.0 - 11.0) Bilirubin 34 µmol/L (3 - 17) ALP 168 u/L (30 - 100) ALT 104 u/L (3 - 40) What process aims to avoid the presentation described in this case?
explanation:
Irradiation
Irradiated blood products are used to avoid transfusion-associated graft versus host disease (TA-GVHD). The patient presents with clinical features that are suggestive of TA-GVHD. These include fever, rash, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, pancytopenia and abnormal liver function tests. TA-GVHD can occur when a patient receives non-irradiated blood products, which may lead to the engraftment of viable donor T-cells. The purpose of irradiating blood products is to damage the DNA within donor T-cells to prevent them from mounting an immune response following transfusion. To mitigate the risk of TA-GVHD, all blood products should undergo irradiation. Immunocompromised patients, such as this one, are particularly at risk of TA-GVHD as they are unable to mount an immune response to the foreign cells in the donor blood. Although irradiation also reduces the risk of TA-GVHD in immunocompromised patients, the risk remains higher than in immunocompetent individuals.

Cross-matching
Cross-matching is a critical procedure that ensures compatibility between the blood types of a patient and a donor before transfusion. Incompatible transfusions can precipitate haemolytic reactions, typically manifesting with symptoms including jaundice, abdominal pain and anaemia. However, these reactions generally occur within 24 hours following the transfusion.

Leukodepletion
Leukodepletion is a filtration process designed to remove nearly all white blood cells from blood products before they are transfused. Its primary aim is to reduce the risk of cytomegalovirus (CMV) transmission through the removal of monocytes and other blood-borne viruses. It is recommended for patients who are immunocompromised, like ours. CMV infection can present in several ways in immunocompromised patients, including colitis and retinitis. However, the case described is more closely aligned with TA-GVHD.

Plasmapheresis
Plasmapheresis refers to a technique where plasma is separated from blood cells in a sample. This process can be employed to produce fresh frozen plasma for transfusions or treat plasma in conditions like Guillain-Barré syndrome before it is returned to the patient's circulation. Plasmapheresis does not serve as a preventative measure against TA-GVHD.

Platelet apheresis
Platelet apheresis involves separating platelets from whole blood. It might be utilised as part of treatment strategies for essential thrombocytopenia or in generating platelet concentrates for transfusion in cases of severe thrombocytopenia. However, platelet apheresis does not play a role in reducing the risk of TA-GVHD.

stem: A 40-year-old female patient diagnosed with sickle cell anaemia had complicated recurrent hospital admissions with a recent episode where she suffered from acute severe pain affecting both her arms, pain when breathing in and out as well as extreme tiredness. She was seen in the haematology clinic as an outpatient to optimise the management of her underlying condition to reduce the incidence of such complications. Which of the following medications should this patient be commenced on?
explanation:
Hydroxycarbamide
Sickle cell patients should be started on long term hydroxycarbamide to reduce the incidence of complications and acute crises. Hydroxycarbamide reduces the frequency of painful episodes and the risk of life-threatening illness or death. However, it can also increase your risk of infections. It is advised not to be taken in pregnancy. Hydroxycarbamide essentially makes your red blood cells bigger, stay rounder and more flexible. Therefore, less likely to turn into a sickle shape. This is achieved by increasing a special kind of haemoglobin called haemoglobin F.

Deferoxamine
Deferoxamine is an iron chelation therapy used in sickle cell disease to enhance iron excretion and removes excessive tissue iron in regularly transfused patients with sickle cell disease.

Folic acid
Folic acid taken regularly in anaemia raises haemoglobin levels and helps provide a healthy reticulocyte response. However, the use of folic acid in patients with sickle cell disease is not well supported by primary literature.

Penicillin V
Penicillin V helps prevent life-threatening infections, particularly in patients who have undergone a splenectomy, which is not the case here.

Vitamin D
Vitamin D deficiency has been shown in 98 per cent of patients with sickle cell disease. As a result of low bone density, patients may develop osteonecrosis, chronic inflammation and related pain. Therefore whilst vitamin D supplementation is important, hydroxycarbamide has a more crucial role in reducing the incidence of complications and acute crises.

stem: A 19-year-old male who emigrated from Ghana as a child presents with an intermittent painful morning erection for the last 5 hours. On examination he has mild splenomegaly. He has never had this problem before and is usually fit and well. Investigations demonstrate: Hb 115 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) MCV 76 fL (80-95) The peripheral blood film shows multiple small red blood cells, a few sickle cells and target cells. What is the most likely genotype for his condition?
explanation:
HbSC
Hb SC is a milder form of sickle disease. Most children in the UK are screened for sickle cell disease, leading to early diagnosis and regular follow up. In HbSC patients have the sickle mutation and the HbC mutation - where a lysine replaces glutamic acid on position 6 of the normal beta chain. The presentation is similar to sickle cell disease but with reduced severity and frequency of symptoms.

HbAA
HbAA is normal and does not cause sickle cell disease or related symptoms.

HbSS
HbSS is severe sickle cell disease, which would typically present with more frequent and severe symptoms.

HbSβ0
HbSβ0 is severe sickle cell disease, similar to HbSS, and would present with more frequent and severe symptoms.

Hbβ/β0
Hbβ/β0 is not a recognized genotype for sickle cell disease.

stem: A 34-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a one-week history of fatigue. There is no evidence of bleeding on systematic inquiry or examination. He has recently completed a course of antimalarial prophylaxis for travel to Uganda. Blood results are as follows: Hb 84 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Reticulocytes 322 * 109/L (50-100) Platelets 182 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 10.8 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Blood film Polychromasia; Frequent blister cell Thick and thin blood films No abnormality detected Direct antiglobulin test (DAT) Weakly positive for IgG (1+) What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
G6PD deficiency
Malaria prophylaxis (e.g. primaquine) can trigger haemolytic anaemia in those with G6PD deficiency. Anaemia with reticulocytosis is suggestive of haemolysis or bleeding. The lack of any obvious bleeding source favours haemolysis in this case. The differential diagnosis for haemolysis is wide including immune and nonimmune mediated mechanisms. The presence of blister cells highly suggests G6PD deficiency since these are a result of oxidative damage which occurs with this condition. They would not be expected with any of the other causes of haemolysis. G6PD deficiency is correct. The presence of haemolysis with blister cells on the blood film is highly suggestive of G6PD deficiency. Furthermore, several antimalarials (e.g. primaquine) are well-known precipitants of a haemolytic crisis in those with G6PD deficiency.

Auto-immune haemolytic anaemia
Auto-immune haemolytic anaemia is incorrect. A positive DAT is associated with autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. However, it is important to remember that this is a non-specific test and can be positive due to a variety of other reasons. The presence of blister cells and exposure to primaquine favours the diagnosis of G6PD deficiency.

Hereditary spherocytosis
Hereditary spherocytosis is incorrect. Although this condition can also present with haemolysis, one would expect to find spherocytes on the blood film.

Malaria
Malaria is incorrect. Although this remains within the differential diagnosis, the absence of malaria parasites on thick and thin blood films makes this an unlikely diagnosis.

Methemoglobinemia
Methemoglobinemia is incorrect. Although methaemoglobinaemia can occur as a consequence of primaquine exposure, it would present with hypoxia, cyanosis, and cardiovascular instability rather than anaemia.

stem: A 73-year-old man visits his general practitioner with a 12-week history of increased lethargy and weight loss. His appetite has reduced over time although he is still trying to eat regularly. His past medical history includes osteoarthritis and mild hypertension. On examination, his observations are recorded and within normal range. His chest sounds are clear and heart sounds are normal. He has a soft and non-tender abdomen. There is palpable splenomegaly and palpable axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy. Investigations: Hb 148 g/L Male: (135-180)) Platelets 200 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 49.3 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Lymphocytes 46.4 * 109/L (0.8 - 5.0) Neutrophils 3.1 * 109/L (2.5 - 7.5) Blood film: Smudge cells. What is the next investigation to order?
explanation:
Immunophenotyping
CLL - immunophenotyping is investigation of choice Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia is the most common leukaemia secondary to a monoclonal expansion of predominantly B cells. Often there are no symptoms and the disease is picked up incidentally on routine blood tests. In other cases, symptoms include anorexia, weight loss, lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly and increased bleeding and infections. The investigation of CLL includes a full blood count, blood film which may show the presence of smudge or smear cells and a bone marrow aspiration to demonstrate infiltration with lymphocytes. Immunophenotyping is an important investigation for diagnosing CLL and has a role in predicting prognosis.

Coomb's test
A positive Coomb's test is not specific for CLL and can be present in multiple other conditions associated with autoimmune haemolytic anaemia.

Cytogenetic testing
Cytogenetic testing is not needed in CLL. Rather, it is an important investigation for other leukaemias such as acute myeloid leukaemia and chronic myeloid leukaemia where certain chromosomal translocations have favourable or less desirable outcomes that can ultimately help determine prognosis and predict treatment.

Immunoglobulin assay
Immunoglobulin levels may be low or normal in patients with CLL. However, immunoglobulin levels can be affected by several other conditions including pre-existing autoimmune deficiencies and paraproteinaemias.

Lymph node biopsy
A lymph node biopsy is an important investigation to consider. However, it is not a diagnosis needed to confirm CLL. Rather, it is an important diagnostic investigation in other haematological malignancies such as lymphoma.

stem: A 48 year old nurse presents with a short history of epistaxis and bleeding gums. You request urgent bloods, the results of which are shown in the table below: Haemoglobin 86 g/L White cells 2.3 x 10^9/L Platelets 18 x 10^9/L Clotting deranged Blood film bilobed large mononuclear cells What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Acute myeloid leukaemia
This is a picture of bone marrow failure secondary to acute myeloid leukaemia. In acute leukaemia a malignant expansion abnormal white cells accumulate in the bone marrow, replacing normal haemopoietic cells. Acute expansion of the myeloid stem line (acute myeloid leukaemia) is more common over the age of 45, in comparison with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia which is mostly seen in children.

Von Willebrand's disease
Von Willebrand's disease may present with epistaxis and bleeding gums in severe cases, but it is rare that there are abnormalities on blood results.

Lymphoma
Lymphoma does not tend to present in this way, but more so with rubbery enlargement of lymph nodes.

stem: A patient with lung cancer has a Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scan to evaluate possible metastatic disease. What does this type of scan demonstrate?
explanation:
Glucose uptake
The correct answer is Glucose uptake. Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scans work by injecting a small amount of radioactive glucose into the body. Cancer cells, being more metabolically active, consume more glucose than normal cells and hence light up on PET scans. This allows for the detection and localisation of cancerous growths in the body.

Cellular proliferation
The first incorrect option is Cellular proliferation. While it's true that cancer cells proliferate rapidly, a PET scan does not directly measure this process. Instead, it measures the metabolic activity of cells as indicated by their glucose consumption. Other imaging techniques such as MRI or CT scans may give an indication about cellular proliferation based on tumour size and growth over time.

Apoptotic activity
The second incorrect option is Apoptotic activity. Apoptosis refers to programmed cell death, which is typically decreased in cancer cells. However, PET scans do not provide information about apoptotic activity. There are other laboratory techniques like flow cytometry or TUNEL assay which can detect apoptosis at a cellular level.

Vascular supply
The third incorrect option is Vascular supply. Although tumours often stimulate the formation of new blood vessels to supply their increased nutrient demands (a process known as angiogenesis), this isn't what a PET scan demonstrates. Angiogenesis can be visualised using other imaging modalities like Doppler ultrasound or contrast-enhanced MRI.

Tyrosine kinase activity
Lastly, Tyrosine kinase activity is also not demonstrated by a PET scan. Tyrosine kinases are enzymes that can be overactive in some types of cancers, leading to uncontrolled cell growth and division. Their activity can be measured in laboratory studies but not through imaging techniques like PET scans.

stem: A 34-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 20 minutes after an episode of acute facial flushing, lip swelling, and dyspnoea. Her symptoms began shortly after eating shellfish. She has allergic rhinitis, and her mother has experienced similar symptoms in the past. Her pulse was initially 122 bpm, her blood pressure was 78/50 mmHg, and she had widespread urticaria. In the ambulance, she received IM adrenaline, and her symptoms improved on the way to the hospital. Blood tests, including mast cell tryptase, were collected immediately after her arrival. Which option is the best next step?
options: Measure mast cell tryptase in 1-2 hours
explanation:
Measure mast cell tryptase in 1-2 hours
This patient's most likely diagnosis is anaphylaxis triggered by shellfish ingestion, evidenced by acute facial flushing, lip swelling, dyspnoea, widespread urticaria, hypotension (78/50 mmHg), and tachycardia (122 bpm) shortly after allergen exposure. Her history of allergic rhinitis and her mother's similar symptoms suggest a familial predisposition to allergic reactions, such as atopy or food allergy. Measuring mast cell tryptase in 1–2 hours is correct because tryptase peaks within this timeframe following mast cell degranulation during anaphylaxis. Samples are collected at three main points: as soon as possible after emergency treatment, 1-2 hours after, and then at least 24 hours later. This helps capture a peak in its levels, distinguishing it from chronic elevation (e.g. systemic mastocytosis), and establishes a baseline. This approach aids future risk assessment, allergen identification, and adrenaline auto-injector prescription.

Measure C1-INH levels in 1-2 hours
Measure C1-INH levels in 1-2 hours is incorrect, as low C1-INH levels are associated with hereditary angioedema (HAE). While HAE can cause facial and airway swelling, it lacks urticaria, does not usually cause hypotension, and develops more gradually. Additionally, her symptoms developing after allergen exposure are more in keeping with anaphylaxis. Even if this patient were to have suspected HAE, C1-INH levels are not routinely measured due to expenses and limited testing capability. Instead, C4 levels are often measured, which are low.

Measure C4 levels in 1-2 hours
Measure C4 levels in 1-2 hours is incorrect as low C4 levels are used to screen for HAE. While HAE can also cause facial and airway swelling, this is non-pruritic, lacks urticaria, does not cause hypotension, and develops more gradually. Additionally, her symptoms developing after eating shellfish are more suggestive of anaphylaxis. While she has a family history of similar symptoms, these likely reflect a familial predisposition to allergy (e.g. atopy or food allergy) rather than HAE. If this patient were to have suspected HAE, C4 levels would be an appropriate screening test, with low levels suggesting its presence.

Measure C4 levels now
Measure C4 levels now is incorrect. Similar to the option above, low C4 levels are associated with HAE, which causes non-pruritic facial and airway swelling without hypotension and urticaria, and develops more slowly, without preceding allergen exposure. While she has a family history of similar symptoms, these likely reflect a familial predisposition to allergy (e.g. atopy or food allergy) rather than HAE. However, if HAE were suspected, C4 levels would be appropriate, with low levels suggesting its presence.

Measure mast cell tryptase now
Measure mast cell tryptase now is incorrect, as this is too early. Mast cell tryptase levels have already been collected, and their levels peak 1-2 hours after symptom onset, followed by a gradual decline over the next 12 hours. Where possible, mast cell tryptase is measured at three points: as soon as possible after emergency treatment starts, 1-2 hours postsymptom onset, and a baseline level > 24 hours later. This approach aids in the identification of a peak in tryptase levels, aiding the diagnosis of anaphylaxis. Collecting a repeat sample now is likely to be too early to detect a significant rise, risking a false-negative result.

stem: A 78-year-old man with a known diagnosis of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL), managed with active monitoring, reports two weeks of increasing fatigue. On examination, he has mild scleral icterus. His blood results are shown below. Hb 85 g/L (135-180) Reticulocytes 250 x 109/L (25-85) Bilirubin 45 µmol/L (<21) LDH 550 U/L (135-214) Direct Antiglobulin Test Positive (IgG) (Negative) What is the most appropriate initial management?
explanation:
Oral prednisolone
The clinical picture of anaemia, reticulocytosis, raised bilirubin, and raised LDH is highly suggestive of haemolytic anaemia. The positive direct antiglobulin test (DAT) with IgG confirms an immune-mediated cause. This is a classic presentation of warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA), which is a well-recognised complication in 10-15% of patients with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL). The first-line treatment for warm AIHA is high-dose oral corticosteroids, such as Oral prednisolone. Steroids work by suppressing the immune system, thereby reducing both the production of autoantibodies and the phagocytosis of antibody-coated red cells by macrophages in the spleen and liver. Treatment is usually initiated promptly to control the haemolysis and improve the anaemia.

FCR chemotherapy
FCR chemotherapy (Fludarabine, Cyclophosphamide, Rituximab) is a standard treatment for CLL itself, but it is not the initial management for this specific complication. The immediate priority is to control the life-threatening autoimmune haemolysis. Furthermore, purine analogues like fludarabine are known to be associated with an increased risk of developing or exacerbating autoimmune cytopenias, including AIHA. Therefore, initiating FCR in this context could potentially worsen the patient's condition and is generally avoided as a first-line approach for CLL-associated AIHA.

Rituximab monotherapy
Rituximab monotherapy is an effective treatment for warm AIHA and is often used as a second-line agent. Rituximab is a monoclonal antibody that targets the CD20 antigen on B-lymphocytes, leading to their depletion and a subsequent reduction in autoantibody production. While effective, its onset of action is slower than corticosteroids, which provide a more rapid immunosuppressive effect. Therefore, according to UK guidelines, rituximab is typically reserved for patients who are refractory to steroids, have a contraindication to them, or become steroid-dependent.

Splenectomy
Splenectomy is a third-line treatment option for patients with warm AIHA who have failed medical therapies. The spleen is a primary site of destruction for antibody-coated red blood cells. Removing the spleen can therefore significantly reduce the rate of haemolysis and improve the anaemia. However, it is a major surgical procedure with associated risks of bleeding, infection (particularly with encapsulated organisms), and thrombosis. It is only considered in refractory cases after less invasive options like corticosteroids and rituximab have been exhausted.

Urgent red cell transfusion
Urgent red cell transfusion is reserved for patients with severe, life-threatening anaemia causing haemodynamic instability (e.g., angina, heart failure, profound hypotension). While this patient is symptomatic, he is stable. Furthermore, cross-matching blood for transfusion can be extremely difficult in warm AIHA because the autoantibodies react with almost all donor red cells. Any transfused red cells are also likely to be rapidly destroyed by the same autoimmune process, providing only transient benefit. The primary goal is to treat the underlying autoimmune process first.

stem: A 54-year-old gentleman is diagnosed with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and is started on chemotherapy. Two days following his first treatment, he presents to the emergency department with nausea, vomiting, and myalgia. On examination, he appears clinically dehydrated. A diagnosis of tumour lysis syndrome (TLS) is suspected. Which of the following would be in keeping with this diagnosis?
explanation:
Low corrected calcium
Low corrected calcium is the only biochemistry result which would be in keeping with TLS. As phosphate precipitates calcium, the serum concentration of calcium becomes low.

Low phosphate
All of the other biochemistry markers are elevated in TLS. Potassium and phosphate are released from the cells, causing both to be high.

Low uric acid
All of the other biochemistry markers are elevated in TLS.

Low lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
All of the other biochemistry markers are elevated in TLS.

Low creatinine
All of the other biochemistry markers are elevated in TLS.

stem: A 25-year-old man is admitted to the Haematology ward, after experiencing fever and rigors at home. He had completed his first cycle of ABVD chemotherapy for Hodgkin's lymphoma the week before. He is taking prophylactic co-trimoxazole and aciclovir, and has been doing so since starting chemotherapy. Asides from this, he takes no regular medications and has no known drug allergies. On initial assessment, his observations are temperature 38.1ºC, respiratory rate 24/minute, heart rate 94 beats per minute, oxygen saturations 96% on room air and blood pressure 116/72mmHg. His blood results are shown below: Hb 140 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 170 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 1.3 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Neuts 0.4 * 109/L (2.0 - 7.0) Lymphs 0.6 * 109/L (1.0 - 3.5) Mono 0.2 * 109/L (0.2 - 0.8) Eosin 0.1 * 109/L (0.0 - 0.4) Na+ 138 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 3.9 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Bicarbonate 24 mmol/L (22 - 29) Urea 4.0 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 70 µmol/L (55 - 120) Which of the following antimicrobial regimens should be started, pending further information from blood culture results?
explanation:
Intravenous piperacillin/tazobactam
Intravenous piperacillin/tazobactam is the empirical antibiotic of choice for neutropenic sepsis, in the absence of contraindications.

Intravenous co-amoxiclav
Intravenous co-amoxiclav by itself would not provide sufficiently broad cover for gram negative organisms, and those with inducible beta-lactamase activity, and is therefore not appropriate as an empirical antibiotic for neutropenic patients.

Intravenous vancomycin, gentamicin and metronidazole
